# Add a server (https://irc-hslu.github.io/orbbecstreamer/docs/client/add-a-server)







Each server you add gets its own card in the side panel, and all servers draw their point clouds in the same 3D view.

## Connect on the server PC [#connect-on-the-server-pc]

The packaged server serves this client itself. The server must be running: after installing, start it with `sudo systemctl start orbbec-streamer`. On the server PC, open `http://127.0.0.1:8080` (or `http://localhost:8080`) in Chrome or Edge. The client asks that page where the server is and which certificate to trust, and adds the server by itself the first time the page loads and no server is listed. A card appears under **Servers**. Select **Remove** to take it away; it stays away after a reload.

The server’s WebTransport gateway starts once a camera is active. If the card shows **Error** at first, start a camera on the server; the client keeps trying. The server only accepts the pages `http://127.0.0.1:8080` and `http://localhost:8080`, so a client opened from another address, such as the development server on port 5173, is refused.

## Connect by typing an address [#connect-by-typing-an-address]

Use this when the client runs somewhere else, for example from a development server. The client connects over WebTransport, a browser connection type for fast, two-way streaming. You need the server’s WebTransport address. The packaged server’s is `https://127.0.0.1:4443/orbbec`; a server on another machine uses its own host name, for example `https://capture-01.local:4443/orbbec`.

1. Start the client and open it. See [Run the client](/docs/client/dev-build).
2. Under **Servers**, type the server’s address into the URL field, which shows `https://host:4443/orbbec` when empty. Replace the host name, port and path with your server’s.
3. Open **Certificate hash (SHA-256), optional** and paste the server’s certificate hash. Skip this only when your browser already trusts the certificate.
4. Select **Connect**.

<img alt="The top of Servers: the URL field with the placeholder https://host:4443/orbbec and Connect, the folded Certificate hash field, the folded Open recording, and Add mock server" src="__img0" />

The form checks the address and the hash before it connects. The address must start with `https://` and must not contain a `#`. The hash is 64 hex digits (capitals, small letters or pairs separated by `:`) or 43 to 44 base64 characters; anything else shows an error under the field and nothing is added.

The packaged server’s certificate is self-signed and lasts 13 days, so browsers don’t trust it by themselves. The hash tells the browser to trust exactly that certificate. On the server PC, run `sudo orbbec-tls status` and copy `sha256Hex` of the `webtransport` entry whose role is `current`. After the certificate is renewed, the old hash no longer works: add the server again with the new one, or use the page of the server PC, which refetches it before every attempt.

The client remembers its servers in this browser, those you add by address (with their hash) and this page’s own server, and adds them again when the page loads. **Remove** on a card forgets it. Recordings aren’t remembered, and if the browser blocks storage nothing is remembered.

If you type the address the page’s own server offers (same host, port and path as **Use this server**) and leave the hash empty, the client uses **Use this server** for you, with the hashes fetched again before every attempt.

## Use the server that served this page [#use-the-server-that-served-this-page]

When the server that served the client offers transport discovery, **Servers** also shows **Use this server**. The client checks this when the page loads. The page must come from an `https://` address, or from `http://127.0.0.1` or `http://localhost` on the server PC. Select **Use this server** to connect without typing an address.

Before every connection attempt, the client asks the page’s own address where the server is and which certificate to trust. A rotated certificate is picked up on the next reconnect. The card shows the address in use, for example `webtransport https://127.0.0.1:4443/orbbec via discovery`.

If the page’s server stops offering discovery before the first connection, the card shows `This page’s server offers no transport discovery: add the server by its URL`, and the client doesn’t retry. Once a connection has worked, the client keeps retrying through brief outages.

## Add the mock server instead [#add-the-mock-server-instead]

The development server has a simulated capture server, the mock server. It behaves like a real server, so you can try every screen without hardware.

1. Start the client with `npm run dev`. See [Run the client](/docs/client/dev-build).
2. Under **Servers**, select **Add mock server**.

The line under the button says `Added a mock server (snapshot only, no media).`: the mock server sends status but no video. Where your checkout has a local copy of the team’s sample recordings, it says `Added a mock server (reference recording).` and also streams that video. See [Sample recordings](/docs/client/developer/test-the-client#sample-recordings). Either way, you can try every card and setup screen. The built copy of the client (`npm run build`) has no mock server.

## What you should see [#what-you-should-see]

A new card appears under **Servers** at once, with the status chip **Connecting**. After a moment, it shows the server’s name, its ID and **Ready** or **Streaming**. The client then asks the server for all its video streams.

If no point cloud appears, your browser may not be able to decode the video. See [Check your browser](/docs/client/browser-requirements).

<img alt="Servers with one card for the Dev mock server: Ready, its server ID and mock address, and a Setup and control only chip because the capture browser can’t decode HEVC" src="__img1" />

[Read a server card](/docs/client/server-card) explains every part of the card.

If the connection drops, the client reconnects by itself and keeps trying. The wait starts at 1 second and doubles with each failed try, up to 30 seconds; each wait is cut by a random 0 to 50 %, so clients don’t all retry at once. The wait starts over at 1 second only after a connection has stayed up for 10 seconds. The client doesn’t retry after you select **Remove**, after a protocol version mismatch, after a conflict, or, in Chrome and Edge, when the site’s security policy blocks the server.

## Fix connection problems [#fix-connection-problems]

A card whose server has never answered shows `N failed attempts; next retry in X s.` under the error. After two failed attempts it adds one hint naming the usual causes, with a link to this section:

* **The certificate isn’t trusted.** Add its hash under **Certificate hash (SHA-256), optional**, or open the client from the server PC’s page and select **Use this server**.
* **This page’s address isn’t allowed by the server.** Open the client from the server’s own https address, or `http://127.0.0.1:8080` on the server PC. See [Serve to browsers](/docs/server/serving).
* **The server isn’t running yet.** Its gateway starts once a camera is active.

A card added by **Use this server** (or by the automatic connect) takes the certificate and allowed address from the server itself, so those two aren’t the cause. After two failed attempts it shows **Server or camera not running** instead: start the server on the server PC with `sudo systemctl start orbbec-streamer`, and make sure a camera is active, because the gateway starts only once a camera is active. The package no longer starts the server when it installs. The card connects by itself once both are running.

The browser doesn’t tell the client which of these it is, so the card can’t say. The hint goes away once the server has answered once; later drops show the plain message below.

### Close messages [#close-messages]

When a connection ends, the card’s close box names why in bold and says what to do. Below it, `last close: …` keeps the raw reason, for example `closed by server (code 4, slow-consumer): control backlog`. Once the connection is back, only the raw reason stays.

| Message                          | What happened                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           | What to do                                                                                                                                                      |
| -------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Connection refused.**          | The connection failed at once. The browser doesn’t say why, so the card can’t either: no server running at that address and port, an untrusted certificate, this page’s address not on the server’s allow-list, a host name the server doesn’t accept, or a server that is full or stopping. In Chrome a closed port fails within milliseconds, exactly like a refusal. | Check the address and the certificate hash, and open the client from the server’s own page. A full server frees up; the client retries after at least 1 second. |
| **Server did not answer.**       | Nothing came back within 10 seconds.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    | Check the address and port, and that the server is running. A firewall that blocks UDP to that port looks the same.                                             |
| **Server closed the session.**   | The server stopped or restarted (close code 0).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         | Nothing; the client reconnects when it is back.                                                                                                                 |
| **Server rejected this client.** | The server found a protocol error in what the client sent (code 1).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     | Update the client or the server so their versions match.                                                                                                        |
| **Server error.**                | A fault on the server (code 2, or a code the protocol doesn’t define).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  | The client reconnects. If it repeats, check the server log.                                                                                                     |
| **Hello took too long.**         | The server got no hello within 10 seconds (code 3).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     | Usually a slow or lossy network; the client reconnects.                                                                                                         |
| **This client fell behind.**     | The client read the server’s messages too slowly (code 4), for example in a busy or throttled tab.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      | Close other heavy tabs; the client reconnects.                                                                                                                  |
| **Server stream failed.**        | A stream write or read failed on the server (code 5), often a network drop.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             | Nothing; the client reconnects.                                                                                                                                 |
| **Connection lost.**             | The connection dropped without a close from the server.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 | Nothing; the client reconnects.                                                                                                                                 |

While the card shows the failed-attempts hint above, the close box shows only its bold reason, so the causes aren’t repeated.

What the browser shows: only the server’s close code (0 to 5) and its reason reach the client. The answer the server gives before a session exists (421 for an unknown host name, 403 for a refused page address, 503 when it is full or stopping, 404 for a wrong path, 400 for a failed upgrade, and a refusal when it has too many connections) never does: the browser reports the same generic failure for all of them, and for an untrusted certificate too.

These messages appear on the server card:

* **Error** status, **Connection refused.** and `last close: transport error: …`: the client couldn’t open the connection.
  * Check that the server is running and that you can reach its host and port over UDP. WebTransport runs over UDP, not TCP. The packaged server’s gateway starts once a camera is active.
  * Check that your browser trusts the server’s certificate: add its hash, or use **Use this server**.
  * Check that the server allows this page’s address. The packaged server accepts `http://127.0.0.1:8080` and `http://localhost:8080` only. See [Serve to browsers](/docs/server/serving).
  * A browser without WebTransport fails this way on every try. See [Check your browser](/docs/client/browser-requirements).
* **`last close: transport error: blocked by this page's Content Security Policy …`**: the site that serves the client doesn’t allow connections to this server’s address (its Content Security Policy `connect-src` doesn’t list it). The browser refuses before it sends anything. In Chrome and Edge the client recognises this and doesn’t retry; other browsers word the refusal differently, so there the card shows a plain `transport error` and the client keeps retrying with backoff. Check the address on the card first. If it’s right, ask whoever deploys the client to add the server’s `https://host:port` to `connect-src`. The policy only changes when the page loads, so reload the page and add the server again. **Reconnect** tries once more, but meets the same policy until you reload.
* **Server did not answer.** and **`connect timeout`**: the server didn’t finish connecting within 10 seconds. It may be unreachable, or it may not answer. Check the server’s logs.
* **`Protocol version mismatch; cannot connect.`**: the server uses another major version of the protocol. Update the client or the server. The client doesn’t retry.
* **`last close: protocol error invalid-transform: …`**, or `invalid-quantization-profile`, `invalid-bundle-descriptor` or `invalid-message`: the server sent data that breaks the protocol, for example a placement that isn’t rigid. The client closes the connection and retries. Check the server’s calibration and placement, and report the text after the code.
* **`last close: internal error: media channel …`** or **`media stream …`**: the client hit a bug while it read that server’s video. It closes only this connection, reconnects and starts again from a fresh snapshot; other servers keep streaming. If it repeats, report the full text.
* **`This server is already open on the card "…"`**: two cards reach the same server, for example once by IP address and once by host name. The message names the other card and says whether it is a live server or a recording. Select **Remove** on that card to show this one.
* **Streaming, but Pairs stays at 0**: a **Setup and control only** chip means your browser can’t decode the video. See [Check your browser](/docs/client/browser-requirements). Otherwise, open **Details** and look at the bundle rows under **Layout**.

These messages appear under the URL field:

| Message                                                          | Fix                                                                                           |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `enter a server URL, e.g. https://127.0.0.1:4443/orbbec`         | Type an address, for example `https://127.0.0.1:4443/orbbec`.                                 |
| `not a URL: …`                                                   | Type a full address, including `https://`.                                                    |
| `WebTransport needs an https: URL, got …`                        | Start the address with `https://`.                                                            |
| `WebTransport URLs cannot have a fragment (#…)`                  | Remove the `#` and everything after it.                                                       |
| `certificate hash: not a SHA-256 hash: expected 64 hex digits …` | Paste the whole hash: 64 hex digits, or 43 to 44 base64 characters. Or leave the field empty. |


# Check your browser (https://irc-hslu.github.io/orbbecstreamer/docs/client/browser-requirements)





The client needs three browser features to show point clouds. Without one of them, the client still connects to servers, shows their status and sets them up, but draws no point clouds.

| Feature                                                                                           | What the client uses it for                                                                                                                            | Without it                                                                                                                            |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| WebTransport                                                                                      | Connecting to a live server                                                                                                                            | Adding a server fails to connect. Recordings still play.                                                                              |
| WebCodecs video decoding with HEVC Main (8-bit) and HEVC Main10 (10-bit), or the built-in decoder | Decoding the colour and depth video                                                                                                                    | No point clouds. Setup and control still work.                                                                                        |
| WebGPU, or WebGL2 as a fallback                                                                   | Drawing the point clouds and blending overlapping cameras. With WebGL2, blending needs 16-bit float render targets, which current graphics cards have. | Without either: no point clouds; setup and control still work. With WebGL2 on software drawing (SwiftShader): no blending by default. |

HEVC is the video format the servers send. At startup the client also checks that your browser decodes it exactly, by decoding two tiny built-in streams and comparing the pixels with a known-good result. A channel that passes is decoded by the browser. A channel that fails is decoded by the client's own WebAssembly HEVC decoder, which runs in one background worker per stream; the client downloads it (about 1.1 MB, 0.37 MB compressed) only when a channel needs it. If that decoder can't load, the channel isn't decoded: the server's card says **Setup and control only** and names the missing HEVC decoding, and its point cloud isn't shown. The browser only turns these features on for secure pages: pages served over `https://`, or from `http://localhost`. The development server at `http://localhost:5173` counts as secure.

## Check what your browser supports [#check-what-your-browser-supports]

1. Start the client and open [http://localhost:5173/](http://localhost:5173/). See [Run the client](/docs/client/dev-build).
2. Read the chips in the header. Hover over a chip for its full sentence; a red or amber chip is also reached with **Tab**:
   * **WebGPU** or **WebGL2**: the 3D backend the client started
   * **WebCodecs**: the browser has WebCodecs. It doesn’t yet say whether it decodes HEVC.
3. If an **i** button follows the chips, select it for the renderer notes, for example `WebGPU not supported`.
4. Add a server or play a recording. If the browser can’t decode that server’s video, its card shows a **Setup and control only** chip.

<img alt="The header: OrbbecStreamer, the protocol version, the theme button, and the green WebGPU and WebCodecs chips" src="__img0" />

With WebGL2, the **View** section says whether it blends; see [Switch blending on or off](/docs/client/viewer#switch-blending-on-or-off). When something is missing:

* **WebGPU that can't draw**: the client uses WebGL2 and says why in an amber notice. See [When WebGPU can't draw](#when-webgpu-cant-draw).
* **No WebGPU and no WebGL2**: a red **No 3D view** chip. Its tip reads `renderer: rendering-incompatible. Rendering incompatible: neither WebGPU nor WebGL2 is available. …`, and the decoder chip turns amber: `Decoding is off`.
* **No WebCodecs**: an amber decoder chip; its tip reads `decoders: WebCodecs VideoDecoder is unavailable: control and setup only.`
* **No HEVC decoding**: the card’s **Setup and control only** chip; its tip reads, for example, `Setup and control only: this browser lacks HEVC colour decoding and HEVC Main10 depth decoding.`

## When WebGPU can't draw [#when-webgpu-cant-draw]

Some browsers offer WebGPU that runs only in software, or that stops as soon as it draws its first frame. One example is Chrome on Linux with an NVIDIA GPU, started without the Vulkan flags. At startup the client checks this: it draws one frame with WebGPU and makes sure the GPU survives it. If WebGPU fails that check, the client uses WebGL2, and an amber notice under the header chips says which case it was:

* **WebGPU runs only in software in this browser, so the 3D view uses WebGL2.**
* **WebGPU did not work in this browser, so the 3D view uses WebGL2.**

WebGL2 blends overlapping cameras too, unless it also draws in software; the **View** section says which.

Each notice ends with a **What to do** link to this section. The **i** button after the chips lists the details, for example `the WebGPU device was lost at its first frame (Device was destroyed.)`. A hardware GPU whose first frame fails gets one more try after half a second before the client switches to WebGL2.

If the GPU stops while you're watching and doesn't recover within 5 seconds, the same place shows **The GPU stopped responding and did not recover, so nothing is drawn. Reload the page to start the 3D view again.** After the reload the client runs its startup check again.

With WebGL2 (also in a headset), the browser can refuse to give the graphics context back. After 5 seconds the same place then shows **The browser lost the graphics context and did not restore it, so nothing is drawn. Reload the page to start the 3D view again.** If it keeps happening, close other tabs that use 3D and restart the browser: Chrome blocks 3D for a page after repeated losses.

To get WebGPU back:

1. In Chrome or Edge, open `chrome://gpu` and check the **WebGPU** line.
2. On Linux with an NVIDIA GPU, start Chrome with `--use-angle=vulkan --enable-features=Vulkan`. WebGPU then runs on the GPU.
3. Reload the client. The header chip says **WebGPU** and the notice is gone.

In 0.1.2 and earlier, the client stayed on WebGPU in this case: no point cloud appeared, **Dropped** counted every pair, and the **View** section kept saying `Preparing blending… plain points meanwhile.`

## Browsers tested so far [#browsers-tested-so-far]

| Browser                                   | Status     | Decoder in use                                           | Expected limits (unverified rows are expectations, not results)                                 |
| ----------------------------------------- | ---------- | -------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Chrome for Testing 155, Linux, NVIDIA GPU | Verified   | Built-in (WASM HEVC)                                     | None found: WebTransport, WebGPU and WebGL2 work; Chrome has no HEVC decoding of its own here.  |
| Google Chrome or Microsoft Edge, Windows  | Not tested | Expected: the browser's own hardware HEVC, else built-in | Whether the 10-bit depth frames can be read is unknown; if not, the built-in decoder is needed. |
| Google Chrome or Microsoft Edge, macOS    | Not tested | Expected: the browser's own hardware HEVC, else built-in | As on Windows.                                                                                  |
| Firefox                                   | Not tested | Expected: built-in (no HEVC in WebCodecs)                | WebGPU depends on version and platform; the WebGL2 fallback blends where the graphics card can. |
| Safari                                    | Not tested | Expected: the browser's own HEVC, else built-in          | WebTransport support depends on the Safari version; without it only recordings play.            |

For a LAN viewer, the page and every server must be on `https:` with a certificate the browser trusts, or the server's certificate hash pinned (see [Add a server](/docs/client/add-a-server)).

Two browsers have been tested. Both report no HEVC decoding of their own, so both use the built-in decoder:

* Headless Chromium 153 on Linux.
* Desktop Google Chrome 155 on Ubuntu 26.04 with an NVIDIA RTX 4090 (2026-10-08). WebGPU and WebGL2 work, and H.264 and VP9 decode, but HEVC colour and Main10 depth do not. Chrome on Linux decodes HEVC through VA-API, and by default there is no VA-API driver for NVIDIA.

With Chrome's default settings on a Linux PC with an NVIDIA GPU, Chrome now shows the point cloud: the client decodes both channels with the built-in decoder. Measured on 2026-10-10 (Google Chrome 155, headless, on a shared PC, an `http://localhost` page, a real 640×576 colour and depth capture played from a recording at 15 frames per second): the built-in decoder is bit-exact against FFmpeg's decode for colour and depth (every 10th frame compared: 45 of each, on that capture and on a 1920×576 NVENC pair), the channels read `wasm / probe-inexact`, and every camera played at 15 frames per second with no dropped frame sets. The cost is CPU. It depends on the video bitrate and, above all, on the clock speed the system picks. Measured on 2026-10-10 and 2026-10-11 (Chrome for Testing 155, headless, an Intel i9-14900KF with the `powersave` governor), with 4 cameras at 15 frames per second at 0.7 Mbit/s colour per camera (the lowest rate seen on the rig), the decoder alone needs 0.16 cores at 5.7 GHz with warm caches. In the running app (load average 0.5 to 2.4) it used 0.53 cores with one concatenated stream and 0.80 cores with one stream per camera, while its CPUs ran at about 2.5 and 1.9 GHz (sampled, approximate): 1.4 to 1.8 times the warm-cache cost, and somewhat more with one stream per camera. So a PC with that setting may need around 0.5 to 0.9 cores for the decoder. These are estimates from a shared PC without capture or encoding running, not the release acceptance test. A computer with fewer or slower cores, or many cameras, may not keep up; the client then drops frames and shows the drops (`decoderOutputDropped` in `droppedFrameSets`). The method and all numbers are in `client/scripts/qa/README.md` (wasm-cpu). The GPU process no longer grows with the number of per-camera streams: measured on 2026-10-11 on the same PC (WebGPU, the same recordings, median of 3 runs, load average 3 to 9), it uses about 0.06 to 0.07 cores for 4 or 8 per-camera streams (it was 0.18 and 0.36 before), and 0.10 to 0.15 for one concatenated stream of 4 or 8 cameras (unchanged). The whole browser at 8 per-camera streams went from 1.38 to 0.83 cores. Hardware decoding is expected on Windows and macOS, but the team has not tested it, nor whether the depth frames can be read. With the nvidia-vaapi-driver package and Chrome started with `--enable-features=VaapiOnNvidiaGPUs`, Chrome 155 decodes HEVC in hardware, but the depth frames can't be read (the decoded 10-bit frames are opaque to the page), so the point cloud still doesn't appear. Tested 2026-10-08 on Ubuntu 26.04, RTX 4090, driver 580. Ubuntu's Chromium snap can't use the driver at all. The next test is Chrome or Edge on Windows, or Safari on macOS. The detailed results are on [Test the client](/docs/client/developer/test-the-client#browsers-tested-so-far).

## Minimum viewer hardware [#minimum-viewer-hardware]

This minimum is provisional; measured on stand-ins, not on real low-end PCs:

* A CPU with 4 cores and 8 threads at 3.0 GHz or faster
* 8 GB of RAM
* A GPU that supports WebGL2
* A current version of Chrome or Edge
* A wired 1 Gbit/s Ethernet connection

The stand-ins ran on one PC (Intel i9-14900KF, RTX 4090), with Chrome for Testing 155 limited to 4 of its CPU threads. Each camera sent a 640×576 colour stream and a 640×576 depth stream at 15 frames per second, decoded by the client's built-in decoder. Every camera played the same content: either a recording of one real camera (colour 2.67 Mbit/s, depth 0.11 Mbit/s) or a synthetic test pattern (colour 2.61 Mbit/s, depth 2.92 Mbit/s). These are not live cameras: a lit, busy live scene costs more to decode. An unrelated job used the GPU (about 80 %) and about 5 CPU cores during every run, so the numbers are pessimistic. Measured on 2026-10-18 between 03:22 and 03:59 UTC, 2 runs each:

| Stand-in for                                            | CPU threads | Cameras | Decoder p95, slower channel (ms) | Dropped | Decoder CPU (cores) | Whole browser (cores) |
| ------------------------------------------------------- | ----------- | ------- | -------------------------------- | ------- | ------------------- | --------------------- |
| 4 cores / 8 threads (2 fast cores with hyper-threading) | 4           | 4       | 3.6                              | 0       | 0.25                | 0.43                  |
| 4 cores / 8 threads, synthetic test pattern             | 4           | 4       | 5.5                              | 0       | 0.40                | 0.57                  |
| 4 cores / 8 threads                                     | 4           | 8       | 5.0                              | 0       | 0.58                | 0.84                  |
| 4 cores / 8 threads, synthetic test pattern             | 4           | 8       | 6.4                              | 0       | 0.84                | 1.10                  |
| Slow CPU (4 efficiency cores, up to 4.4 GHz)            | 4           | 8       | 5.4                              | 0       | 0.67                | 1.06                  |
| Slow main thread (4 threads, main thread slowed 4×)     | 4           | 4       | 4.4                              | 0       | 0.28                | 1.21                  |
| WebGL2 instead of WebGPU, same GPU                      | 4           | 8       | 5.7                              | 0       | 0.59                | 1.00                  |

Every configuration kept 15 frames per second on every camera, with no dropped frame sets. The WebGL2 row runs on the same RTX 4090: it tests the WebGL2 code path, not a weak GPU, which can't be emulated. The client tells servers it can run up to 16 decoders at once (8 cameras). That is the most the measurements tested, not a measured CPU limit, and it was measured on stand-in cores on a PC with an RTX 4090 under unrelated background load. It still reports pictures up to 4096×4096. With the built-in decoder, a picture larger than 3840×2160 in area is refused as soon as the server announces it, before any video arrives, and the card says **Setup and control only** with the reason (see [Fix browser problems](#fix-browser-problems)). A limit of 5120×1152 has been derived from the measured decode cost, but it was not measured directly; it will be checked with real multi-camera pictures before it changes. The full results are in `client/scripts/qa/perf/results/2026-10-18-viewer-floor/`.

## Fix browser problems [#fix-browser-problems]

These are the common browser problems and their fixes:

* **No 3D view on a desktop browser**: hardware acceleration may be off. Turn on **Use graphics acceleration when available** in the browser settings. In Chrome or Edge, open `chrome://gpu` to check the WebGL2 and WebGPU status.
* **Points don't blend and a notice says WebGPU did not work**: see [When WebGPU can't draw](#when-webgpu-cant-draw) and the **View** section's status line ([When blending turns itself off](/docs/client/viewer#when-blending-turns-itself-off)).
* **A camera's video stops decoding in the browser**: if the browser's own decoder fails on one stream, or keeps giving depth frames without 10-bit values, the client moves that stream to the built-in decoder. The stream keeps going from its next keyframe. Other cameras keep the browser's decoder, and the next stream of the same camera tries the browser's decoder again. Only when streams from two different cameras or servers fail does the client use the built-in decoder for that channel for the rest of the page's life. The console shows `[decode path]` warnings such as `Decode path: one depth stream switched to the built-in decoder (WebCodecs decoder failed; …)`. If the built-in decoder can't load either, the card shows **1 bundle off · decoder failed**.
* **Every server card says the browser lacks HEVC decoding**: this browser can't decode HEVC exactly, and the built-in decoder didn't load. Open the browser's console: a `[decode path]` warning reads `Depth/colour cannot be decoded in this browser: the built-in decoder failed to load (<reason>)`. The reason is `HTTP 404` when the decoder file is missing from the server, `…failed its integrity check…` when the file was changed, or `blocked by the page's content security policy` when the page's policy lacks `'wasm-unsafe-eval'` in `script-src`. Fix the cause and reload the page; the client doesn't try again until then. You can still use the client to set up servers.
* **A card says "Setup and control only: the picture 9000×576 is larger than the built-in decoder takes (max 8192 on a side, 3840×2160 area)"**: the built-in decoder takes pictures up to 8192 pixels on a side and 3840×2160 pixels in area (an 8-camera concatenated picture of 640×576 tiles is 5120×576 and fits). The card names the size the server announced; when the browser's own decoder was asked instead, it says "was refused by this browser's decoder (it may be too large)". The console also shows a `warn` line naming the bundle and channel. In the concatenated layout a server sends exactly one bundle, so 8 cameras mean one 5120-wide picture; a recording manifest with two bundles in the concatenated layout is refused with `Concatenated layout must expose exactly one bundle`.
* **Your server sets a content security policy**: the built-in decoder needs `script-src 'self' 'wasm-unsafe-eval'` and `worker-src 'self'`. It needs no other change, no cross-origin isolation headers and no `SharedArrayBuffer`.
* **Nothing works when you open the client from another computer**: plain `http://` pages are only secure on `localhost`. Open the client on the machine that runs it. A packaged install can also serve viewers on the LAN over HTTPS, on port 8443. See [Remote viewers on the LAN](/docs/getting-started/install-package#remote-viewers-on-the-lan).


# Calibrate the floor (https://irc-hslu.github.io/orbbecstreamer/docs/client/calibrate-floor)



The floor step measures where the floor is, in the server’s own frame, from the running cameras. It is there only when the server offers it; a server that doesn’t offer it shows no **Floor** section and no floor chip. Measuring needs the operator role and the setup lock, like the other setup steps. A viewer sees the status only.

The measured floor is a plane. Nothing moves when you commit it. To bring the cloud level, use **Level to floor** (see below), which opens a placement draft that you commit in **Placement**.

## Measure the floor [#measure-the-floor]

1. Open the setup view: select **Set up** on the card. The session chip must read **Active**.
2. The server’s camera pose must be **valid**. Otherwise **Calibrate floor** is off, with the tip `Needs a valid camera pose first.` The cameras must also be running.
3. In **Floor**, select **Calibrate floor**. The state chip reads **running**.
4. While it runs, a line shows the best candidate so far, for example `candidate 4.2 mm, 91 % inliers (12 of 20 frames)`. Nothing is in force yet.
5. When the run is solved, **Commit** appears next to **Cancel**. Select **Commit** to keep the floor, or **Cancel** to throw the run away.

After **Commit**, the chip reads for example **valid · r2**, and the numbers below it are those of the committed floor:

| Number           | Meaning                                                                                                                      |
| ---------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **residual**     | How far the points on the floor are from the plane, in mm. Above 10 mm it is marked `above the 10 mm target`.                |
| **inlier share** | The share of sampled points that lie on the plane.                                                                           |
| **gravity gate** | The angle between the plane and the server’s gravity reference, in degrees. `no gravity reference` when the server has none. |
| **tilt**         | The angle between the floor and level in the scene, with the server’s placement applied.                                     |
| **height**       | The floor’s height above the scene’s ground, with the placement applied, in mm.                                              |

The server card shows a **Floor** chip next to **Pose** and **Depth**, for example **Floor valid · r2** or **Floor stale**.

## When it fails [#when-it-fails]

A failed run shows the stage and the server’s text, for example `Stage: no plane.` or `Stage: too few inliers.` The stage is one of `not enough depth`, `no plane`, `normal outside gravity gate` and `too few inliers`. The text after it is the server’s own. Select **Calibrate floor** to try again; the previous committed floor stays in force.

## When the cameras are recalibrated [#when-the-cameras-are-recalibrated]

A new camera pose makes the floor **stale**: the old plane no longer matches the cameras. The section says `The cameras were recalibrated; measure the floor again.` The old numbers stay on screen. Select **Calibrate floor**.

## Level to floor [#level-to-floor]

**Level to floor** opens a placement draft that makes the measured floor level and puts it at the scene’s ground, keeping the server’s yaw. It is a draft:

* Nothing is sent. Review it in **Placement**, then select **Commit** there. See [Place a server in the scene](/docs/client/placement-editing).
* After you commit a floor, the client opens this draft by itself: `A level placement draft is open; review and commit it in Placement.`
* If you have unsaved placement edits, they are kept and the client says so. Select **Level to floor** to replace them.
* If the measured floor points down or sideways in the current placement, there is no draft: `The measured floor points down in this placement; level it by hand.` **Level to floor** is off with the same reason.

## Correct the floor by hand [#correct-the-floor-by-hand]

If the level draft is close but not right, nudge it in the Floor section, under **Correct by hand**:

* **Pitch** ±0.5°. Plus lifts the far side of the cloud (away from you along +Z).
* **Roll** ±0.5°. Plus lifts the +X side.
* **Height** ±1 cm. Plus lifts the whole cloud.

**Tilt** and **Height** next to the buttons show the measured floor under the draft, live. Nudge until both read 0.

These buttons edit the placement draft (they open one if none is open). They never commit: `Adjusts the placement draft; commit it in Placement.` The rotation turns about the floor point, not the scene origin, so the cloud does not swing. Yaw is never changed. The buttons are off without a measured floor, for a viewer, and while the draft is being committed; each says why.

## Use a keyboard or screen reader [#use-a-keyboard-or-screen-reader]

**Calibrate floor**, **Commit**, **Cancel**, **Level to floor** and the **Pitch**, **Roll** and **Height** nudges are buttons in the tab order. Unavailable ones stay reachable and name their reason. When **Commit** or **Cancel** go away, focus moves to **Calibrate floor**. Screen readers announce, without moving focus, that the floor was measured and waits for **Commit**, a failure with its stage, that the floor is stale, and the result of the level draft.

See also [Show the floor](/docs/client/what-you-can-tweak#view-section) in the 3D view.


# Calibrate depth (https://irc-hslu.github.io/orbbecstreamer/docs/client/calibration)







The server sends depth as a video in which each pixel is one of 1024 codes, and the client turns each code back into a distance. A depth-quantization calibration measures the depths your cameras see and produces a new code-to-distance mapping, called a **result**. The result comes into force only when you commit it, and then every client uses it.

Each calibration section in the setup view has a state chip, for example **valid · r3**: the state (`missing`, `valid`, `stale`, `running` or `failed`) and the revision in force. Hover over it for the server’s message. Only depth quantization works in the client today. A solved run stays **running** until you commit it; the server sends a result only when you commit or when the run fails.

## Depth quantization [#depth-quantization]

Open the setup view first: select **Set up** on the card. The session chip must read **Active**.

1. Select **Start**. The state chip turns **running**.

2. Watch the progress, shown only on the client that holds the lock:

   * **elapsed**, **valid samples**, **observed range** and **reconstruction error** (how far distances rebuilt from the codes are off)
   * **Depth codes**: how many pixels had each code from 2 to 1022. **Log**, the default, keeps small counts visible; **Linear** compares the peaks. The chips under it count the special codes: invalid (`0`), below minimum (`<min`) and above maximum (`>max`).

   <img alt="Depth quantization during a run: the running chip, Cancel available, the four numbers and the Depth codes histogram" src="__img0" />

3. Wait until the run is solved. The chip stays **running** with the old revision, **Commit** becomes available, and the box says `Solved: awaiting commit, not in force until committed.`

   <img alt="The Depth quantization section after a run: the chip still reads running with the old revision, Commit is highlighted, the box says Solved: awaiting commit, not in force until committed, elapsed (last run) 5.5 s, and the final histogram with the log scale selected" src="__img1" />

4. Select **Commit**. A moment later the chip shows **valid** at the new revision, on every client.

If the run fails, the chip keeps its revision (a first calibration turns **failed**) and the box says `The last run produced no result to commit: <reason>. Revision <n> stays in force.`

To stop a run, select **Cancel**. Nothing is committed. Leaving setup does the same: it cancels the run and discards a solved or ready result, and the setup view says `The client discarded the uncommitted depth quantization result.` The reasons an unavailable button shows as its tip:

| Reason                                                                            | Meaning                                                                                         |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `the setup session is not active`                                                 | You don’t hold the lock                                                                         |
| `the depth-quantization calibration is running`                                   | **Start** waits until the run ends, **Commit** until it has a result or reads `awaiting commit` |
| `a depth-quantization commit was already accepted; waiting for the server update` | **Commit** was accepted; the new revision follows                                               |
| `the depth-quantization calibration is not running`                               | Nothing to cancel                                                                               |
| `no accepted depth-quantization result to commit`                                 | Run the calibration first                                                                       |

## Camera pose [#camera-pose]

The section shows its state chip and a red `TODO`. Camera-pose calibration isn’t in the client yet; the server can run it from its own console. See [Camera calibration](/docs/server/camera-calibration).

## Network [#network]

The section shows its state chip and **Not available yet**.

## Fix calibration problems [#fix-calibration-problems]

* **The result never came into force**: a result needs **Commit**. If you left setup or lost the lock first, the client threw the result away. After **Leave** or a forced exit, the box in the setup view says `The client discarded the uncommitted depth quantization result.` Run the calibration again and commit it.
* **You were forced out in the middle of a run**: the client committed nothing. When you’re back in setup, check the state chip: if it still shows **running**, the run went on without you. See [Set up a server](/docs/client/setup-workspace).
* **`Start rejected (<code>): <message>`**, or the same for Cancel or Commit: the server refused the request. The code and message come from the server.
* **`Commit failed (timeout): …`**: the server didn’t answer in time. The state chip tells you whether the new revision is in force. If it isn’t, and the result still shows, select **Commit** again.
* **The state shows `failed`**: the run failed, and there is nothing to commit. Start a new run.
* **`The last run produced no result to commit: <message>. Revision 3 stays in force.`**: the run was cancelled or failed. Start a new run.
* **`histogram: not reported by the server`**: the server sent no histogram. The numbers above it still apply.
* **`histogram: depth histogram has N bins, expected 1024`**: the server sent a histogram of the wrong size, so the client doesn’t draw it.
* **Commit accepted, but the state chip still shows the old revision**: the new revision comes into force with the server’s next update. If it doesn’t follow, check the card for a **resynchronising** chip or a lost connection.


# Run the client (https://irc-hslu.github.io/orbbecstreamer/docs/client/dev-build)





You serve the client from your own machine with a development server: install it once, start the server, then open the page in your browser.

## Install and start the client [#install-and-start-the-client]

You need Node.js 24 with npm, and a copy of the OrbbecStreamer repository.

1. Install the client’s dependencies. Run this in the repository’s top folder:

   ```bash
   cd client
   npm ci
   ```

2. Start the development server. Run this in the `client` folder:

   ```bash
   npm run dev
   ```

3. Open [http://localhost:5173/](http://localhost:5173/) in your browser.

Leave the terminal open while you use the client. To stop the server, press **Ctrl+C** in that terminal.

## What you should see [#what-you-should-see]

The terminal shows `VITE v6.4.3  ready in 300 ms`, then `➜  Local:   http://localhost:5173/`. The version and time may differ. The browser shows the empty 3D view, reading `No servers yet`, and the side panel on the right:

<img alt="The client right after it opens: the empty 3D view reading No servers yet, Connect a server or open a recording, and the side panel with the header, View, Servers with the URL field, Open recording and Add mock server, and an empty World anchors" src="__img0" />

[Tour of the client](/docs/client/tour) explains each part of the screen.

## Build a static copy [#build-a-static-copy]

You don’t need this step to use the client. It makes a folder of static files you can serve with any web server. Run this in the `client` folder:

```bash
npm run build
npm run preview
```

`npm run build` checks the code and writes the files to `client/dist/`. `npm run preview` serves that folder at [http://localhost:4173/](http://localhost:4173/). The built copy has no **Add mock server** button.

## Troubleshooting [#troubleshooting]

These are the problems people hit most when starting the client:

* **`Error: Port 5173 is already in use`**: another development server is running. Stop it, or start this one on another port and open that port instead. In the `client` folder:

  ```bash
  npm run dev -- --port 5174
  ```

* **`Error: ENOSPC: System limit for number of file watchers reached`**: Linux limits how many files one user can watch, and every program you run shares that limit (editors, other development servers, other checkouts). The client itself watches only a few hundred files. Raise the limit, then start the server again:

  ```bash
  sudo sysctl fs.inotify.max_user_watches=524288
  echo 'fs.inotify.max_user_watches=524288' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/60-inotify.conf
  ```

  The first line takes effect now; the second keeps it after a restart. Stopping other development servers or editors also frees watchers.

* **`npm: command not found`**: Node.js is installed without npm on this machine. Install npm with your Node.js distribution. Once `client/node_modules/` exists, you can also start the server without npm. In the `client` folder:

  ```bash
  ./node_modules/.bin/vite
  ```

* **The header shows a red No 3D view chip**: your browser can’t draw 3D. See [Check your browser](/docs/client/browser-requirements).

* **Nothing works when you open the page from another computer**: the development server only answers on this computer (`localhost`). Browsers also turn off the features the client needs on plain `http://` pages that aren’t `localhost`. Open the client on the machine that runs it, or serve it over HTTPS with a lab certificate: see [Serve the dev pages over HTTPS](/docs/client/developer/test-the-client#serve-the-dev-pages-over-https).


# Calibration quality API (https://irc-hslu.github.io/orbbecstreamer/docs/client/developer/calibration-quality)



The client keeps the quality of a server's calibration beside the calibration state and exports it for the Operator Console from one React-free module, `client/src/app/calibrationQualityApi.ts`. It follows change 0045 (wire format §11 and §13, feature `calibration-quality`). Everything is diagnostic: the figures never change how media is read.

## Turn it on [#turn-it-on]

Offer the feature on the runtime that should have it:

```ts
startAppRuntime(container, { role: 'operator', features: [CALIBRATION_QUALITY_FEATURE] });
```

The main page offers it already. The server grants it only for protocol minor 2 or later. Check the result with `isCalibrationQualityNegotiated(connection.state)`. Without it every selector returns `[]` or `null`, a quality field that arrives anyway is dropped, and `fetchCalibrationReport` fails with `unsupported-by-server` without sending anything.

## Read the state [#read-the-state]

Read from `connection.state` and again on `connection.onStateChange`.

| Selector                             | Returns                                                                                                                                                                      |
| ------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `calibrationAdvisories(state, kind)` | The advisory codes of the committed record of `kind`, most important first. They change only with a commit or a server restart, never during a run.                          |
| `committedPoseQuality(state)`        | The committed camera-pose figures (`PoseQuality`, no per-view list), or `null` when none is known. `quality-unknown` in the advisories says why.                             |
| `runPoseQuality(state)`              | During a camera-pose run, the last solve attempt (passed or failed) with its per-view list, or `null` before the first attempt. Cleared when the run ends.                   |
| `lastPoseResultQuality(state)`       | `{accepted, revision, quality}` of the last camera-pose result, or `null`. A failed result may carry the last attempt's figures or `null`. Cleared when the next run starts. |
| `cameraQualityOf(quality, cameraId)` | The figures of one camera, or `null`.                                                                                                                                        |
| `pairQualityOf(quality, a, b)`       | The figures of a camera pair, in either order, or `null`.                                                                                                                    |

Pixel figures are in pixels of the camera's observation image (`imageSize` and `observationImage` of the camera figures).

## Show advisories [#show-advisories]

`describeAdvisories(codes)` returns `{code, title, nextStep, known}` for each code, in the server's order. The text covers every code of the contract table. A code the client does not know is shown as is, with an empty `nextStep` and `known: false`.

## Read a report [#read-a-report]

```ts
const fetched = await fetchCalibrationReport(connection, 'camera-pose');
if (fetched.ok) show(fetched.reply.report); // null: nothing committed, or no report for that revision
```

* Reports exist for `camera-pose`, `depth-quantization` and `floor`. `floor` also needs the `floor` feature.
* The call needs the `operator` role and no lease. A viewer gets `{ok: false, reason: 'rejected', code: 'role-required'}`. A spent command budget gets `code: 'rate-limited'`. Neither ends the session.
* The report is the one of exactly `reply.revision`. During a run it is the pre-run report.
* `onCalibrationReport(connection, listener)` is the raw subscription to every reply of this connection.

## Try it against the mock [#try-it-against-the-mock]

See [mock server](/docs/client/developer/mock-server). `?mockQuality=1` gives clean figures and reports, `?mockQuality=advisory` gives advisories, and `?mockQuality=legacy` gives records without reports.


# Cards check (https://irc-hslu.github.io/orbbecstreamer/docs/client/developer/cards-check)



The cards check (`client/dev/cards-check.html`, code in `client/src/dev/cardsCheck.tsx` and `client/src/dev/cardsScenario.ts`) is a dev-only page for the [server cards](/docs/client/server-card). It is never part of the production build.

It runs two clients, **Client A** and **Client B**, against one [mock server](/docs/client/developer/mock-server), and shows each client’s server cards in its own column. The cards are the app’s own cards. The scripted card actions (lock, refresh, shared updates, reconnect) go through the same model function as the card buttons. The calibration and placement steps (4 and 5) call client A’s connection directly; the setup workspace has its own page, the [setup check](/docs/client/developer/setup-check). Nothing is drawn in 3D: each client has a GPU-free renderer.

The mock serves the sample recordings when `client/reference/hevc-web/` exists, decoded by the dev pages’ synthetic decoder. These recordings aren’t published; without them the mock is snapshot-only, with no media.

## Run the check [#run-the-check]

Start the dev server in `client/`:

```bash
npm run dev
```

Open this URL:

```text
http://localhost:5173/dev/cards-check.html?autorun=1
```

URL parameters:

| Parameter   | Effect                                                                 |
| ----------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `autorun=1` | Run the scripted scenario on load. Without it, press **Run scenario**. |
| `media=0`   | Use a snapshot-only mock even when the recordings exist.               |

The scenario, in order:

1. Both clients connect.
2. A acquires the lock. B shows `held by Client A (…)`, and B’s **Acquire lock** is unavailable with the reason `the lock is held by Client A`.
3. B sends an acquire anyway, through the model function the button calls (the unavailable button itself sends nothing). The mock server refuses it, and the page log (not B’s card) shows `Client B: Acquire lock rejected (lock-held): setup lock held by Client A`. `lock-held` is the mock server’s code; a real server may use another.
4. B turns shared updates off, and A commits a placement. A placement commit doesn’t restart the streams, and the payload is withheld from B. B fetches the full state by itself when the notice arrives, so it still gets the new placement.
5. A runs a depth-quantization calibration. B shows it `running`. The run is solved and waits for a commit, with no result yet. A commits: the result is withheld from B, and B fetches the full state by itself on the commit’s revision change, so B shows the calibration `valid` at a new revision and its metadata is not stale.
6. A releases the lock. B acquires it (A shows `held by Client B (…)`), then releases it.
7. The mock drops B’s session. B’s card shows `error` and `reconnect scheduled`, and B’s **Reconnect** restores the session. With the sample recordings, the step also waits until B’s new session uploads frames and its bundle shows `ready, drawing`.

Buttons for trying things by hand:

* **Drop A’s session** and **Drop B’s session**: the mock server loses that client’s session.
* **Expire the lease**: the mock server expires the current lock.
* **Pause for setup** and **Stop streaming**: server-side streaming changes.

The card buttons work as in the app.

## What you should see [#what-you-should-see]

* The page ends with `body[data-state]` set to `done`, the log line `verdict: 7 steps passed`, and both columns showing a live card.
* `window.__cardsCheckReport` holds the report: `state`, `media`, `steps[]` (`name`, `ok`, `detail`), `log`, `errors` and `verdict`. The same JSON is in the collapsed “report JSON” panel.
* Recorded runs, 2026-09-28, headless Chromium 153 on Linux, with the sample recordings:
  * first run: `done`, 7 of 7 steps;
  * two reruns after the per-session counts fix: `done`, 7 of 7 steps, no errors. The last step reported B at `decoded 1, uploaded 1, dropped 0 this session`. A screenshot a moment later showed both columns `ready, drawing`, with decoded pairs equal to uploaded on each card (A 35 / 35, B 12 / 12).

Counts on this page work like this. Both clients are wired the same way: a GPU-free renderer that accepts every upload and draws nothing. The counts are per session, so after B’s Reconnect they start again from zero, while A’s keep growing. A card that shows **Pairs** 0 and `ready, no frame yet` under **Details** right after the reconnect has not received its new session’s first frames yet.

The same scenario runs in Node on a simulated clock as part of `npm test` (`client/src/tests/serverCards.test.ts`).

## Fix check problems [#fix-check-problems]

* **`failed` with `timed out waiting for: …`**: the step named in `verdict` did not reach the expected card state within 8 s. The text after it shows both cards’ status and lock line at that moment.
* **`failed` with `watchdog: not done after 60 s`**: the run hung. Reload the page, and check the browser console.
* **`media` is `snapshot only, no media` although you want frames**: the sample recordings in `client/reference/hevc-web/` are missing or incomplete; `fallbackReason` in the report says which. These recordings aren’t published, so most readers get a snapshot-only mock. The scenario doesn’t need media; the counts stay at 0. See [Sample recordings](/docs/client/developer/test-the-client#sample-recordings).


# Developer options (https://irc-hslu.github.io/orbbecstreamer/docs/client/developer/developer-options)



These options have no control in the client UI. A developer sets them in code, and some through the render check’s query parameters. The app uses the defaults below. For the controls users can change, see [What you can tweak](/docs/client/what-you-can-tweak).

## Point settings [#point-settings]

`RenderSettings`, passed as `settings` in `PointCloudRendererOptions` or changed with `PointCloudRenderer.setSettings` (`client/src/rendering/pointCloudRenderer.ts`, ranges in `client/src/rendering/splats.ts`). They apply to WebGPU and WebGL2. The render check takes the query parameter in brackets; see [Test the client](/docs/client/developer/test-the-client).

| Setting                          | Default  | Range             | Meaning                                                                                             |
| -------------------------------- | -------- | ----------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `pointSize` (`pointSize`)        | 2        | 1 or more         | Dot size in framebuffer pixels, in screen mode. On a display scaled to 200 %, 2 pixels look like 1. |
| `pointSizeMode` (`sizeMode`)     | `screen` | `screen`, `world` | `world` sizes each dot by its depth pixel’s footprint.                                              |
| `worldPointScale` (`worldScale`) | 1.5      | 0 or more         | Scale of the footprint in world mode                                                                |
| `maxPointSize` (`maxSize`)       | 16       | 1 or more         | Largest dot in world mode, in framebuffer pixels                                                    |
| `splatShape` (`shape`)           | `square` | `square`, `round` | Dot shape                                                                                           |
| `debugView` (`debug=1`)          | `false`  |                   | Draws below-range codes blue and above-range codes red                                              |

The blend settings are in the same object; the app exposes them in its **View** section.

## Renderer options [#renderer-options]

`PointCloudRendererOptions`, fixed when the renderer is created:

| Option                  | Default     | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| ----------------------- | ----------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `engine`                | `auto`      | `auto` picks WebGPU when an adapter exists, else WebGL2. `webgpu` or `webgl2` forces one.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| `renderMode`            | `on-demand` | `on-demand` draws only when something changed. `continuous` draws every animation frame.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| `parkWhenIdle`          | `true`      | With `on-demand`, the render loop stops after one animation frame without a draw and restarts on the next change or camera input. An idle view then costs no animation frames and no GPU submissions. Never stops in WebXR or with `continuous`. A host that moves the camera from code calls `requestRender()`.                                                                                                                                  |
| `computePoints`         | `true`      | The WebGPU compute path, which blending needs. `false` keeps plain dots. Ignored with WebGL2.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| `webgl2Blend`           | `'auto'`    | Blending on WebGL2, with the same formulas as WebGPU, while `blend` is on. `'auto'`: on where the GPU can do it, with the checks and the automatic fallback below. `true`: always on, no checks (tests, the render check). `false`: plain dots. Needs 16-bit float render targets; desktop only (WebXR keeps plain dots). `stats().webgl2Blend` and `stats().drawPathNote` say whether it draws and why. See [WebGL2 blending](#webgl2-blending). |
| `antialias`             | `false`     | Multisample antialiasing                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| `desynchronized`        | `true`      | Low-latency WebGL2 canvas, which may tear                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| `preserveDrawingBuffer` | `false`     | Keeps the drawing buffer for canvas readback, for dev pages and screenshots                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |

### WebGL2 blending [#webgl2-blending]

With `webgl2Blend`, WebGL2 views look like WebGPU's blended view, and `drawPath` reads `webgl2-blend`. On the lab machine the render check's synthetic scenes match WebGPU on at least 99.8 % of the compared pixels, within 3/255, mean colour difference (CIEDE2000) at most 0.02.

With `'auto'`, the renderer decides when to blend:

| Case                                                                                                        | What happens                                                 | `drawPathNote`                                                                                                                     |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| No 16-bit float render targets (`EXT_color_buffer_float` or `EXT_color_buffer_half_float`)                  | Plain dots, for good                                         | `16-bit float targets unavailable`                                                                                                 |
| The browser names a software renderer (SwiftShader, llvmpipe)                                               | Plain dots until the user forces blending                    | `SwiftShader: blending off by default` (others: `software renderer: blending off by default`)                                      |
| The browser hides the renderer name (no `WEBGL_debug_renderer_info`, or a generic name such as `Apple GPU`) | Blending stays on only if the start-up check passes          | `checking the blending cost`, then nothing, or the reason it went off; each with `; pass timing unavailable` without a timer query |
| A named GPU                                                                                                 | Blending on                                                  | nothing, or `pass timing unavailable` without a timer query                                                                        |
| The blending passes take more than 40 % of the frame time for 2 s                                           | Plain dots until **Blend** is switched off and on, or forced | `blending off: over 40 % of the frame budget (… of … ms)`                                                                          |
| A render target can't be drawn into                                                                         | Plain dots, for good                                         | e.g. `R16UI weight target incomplete (status 0x8cdd): blending off`                                                                |
| WebXR                                                                                                       | Plain dots (blending in XR comes later)                      | `XR draws the nearest point (no blending in XR yet)`                                                                               |

How it measures:

* **Timer query** (`EXT_disjoint_timer_query_webgl2`, Chrome on the desktop): the GPU time of each blending pass, sampled one frame at a time and never waited on. `stats().webgl2Blend.passMs` holds the recent medians per pass (`weight`, `visibility`, `accumulation`, `resolve`, `total`).
* **Start-up check**, without a timer query (Quest, Safari) or with a hidden renderer name: about 1 s with blending, then 1 s with plain dots (each from its first counted frame, and at least 12 drawn frames), comparing the time between animation frames. It runs only while the view draws anyway, and never stalls the GPU. It only sees frames that miss the display refresh, so `drawPathNote` says `pass timing unavailable`.
* The frame budget is the display's frame time, but at least 1/60 s (and at most 1/30 s): on a 144 Hz screen the limit stays 6.7 ms, not 2.8 ms. The frame time is estimated from animation frames that drew nothing (1/60 s until known). Babylon's own GPU frame-time capture (Inspector) pauses the timing.
* Known limit: when fewer than 2 frames per second are drawn, neither the fallback nor the start-up check can decide; blending stays as it is.

`forceWebgl2Blend()` (the **Blend anyway** button in the **View** section) turns blending on until the page reloads, past the SwiftShader default and the fallback. A render target that reads incomplete for one frame (Chrome does this for a fresh R16UI target in about half the runs) draws plain dots for that frame and is checked again; only after 3 frames does blending go off.

Measured cost (synthetic scenes, NVIDIA RTX 4090 only, Chrome for Testing 155, 2026-10-18, operator freeze 10:03-10:35 UTC, `perf/blend3-freeze.sh` 3 runs, medians; an unrelated background job was present but idle). GPU ms is weight + visibility + accumulation + resolve, each the median of the timer samples in a 20 s window (30 s for the mock servers).

* **Idle clock**: the card chose its own clock: P8 (210 MHz SM, 405 MHz memory) in almost every sample. The 8 × 1920×576 blend scene raised it to P5 (about 705 MHz).
* **Clock keeper on**: a separate GPU load (`perf/clockguard.mjs`) held P2 (2670 MHz, memory 10251 MHz) in every sample and shared the GPU with the scene. The per-pass medians are not inflated by it, but per-frame totals and p95s can be, and frame times change (68 against 60 fps on light scenes).

| Scene                     | GPU ms, idle clock | GPU ms, clock keeper on | `'auto'` at 60 Hz (limit 6.7 ms), idle clock |
| ------------------------- | ------------------ | ----------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| 1 camera, 640×576         | 1.33               | 0.12                    | keeps blending                               |
| 2 cameras                 | 1.80               | 0.18                    | keeps blending                               |
| 4 cameras                 | 2.70               | 0.34                    | keeps blending                               |
| 3 mock servers with media | 4.51               | 0.42                    | keeps blending                               |
| 8 cameras at 1920×576     | 12.2               | 3.17                    | falls back after 2 s                         |

`'auto'` measures live: it reads the pass timings of the running view, so it judges the clock the card really uses. At the idle clock, 1-4 cameras stay under the 6.7 ms limit; the large rig falls back unless the card runs faster (at full clock it took 3.17 ms and would keep blending). Weaker GPUs are expected to fall back with fewer cameras (not measured).

Frame times at the idle clock, nearest -> blend (compare only within one setting):

| Scene                     | fps          | frame p50 / p95 ms              |
| ------------------------- | ------------ | ------------------------------- |
| 1 camera                  | 60.4 -> 60.5 | 16.66 / 16.79 -> 16.66 / 16.82  |
| 2 cameras                 | 60.4 -> 60.2 | 16.66 / 16.83 -> 16.66 / 19.24  |
| 4 cameras                 | 50.4 -> 43.4 | 19.85 / 21.18 -> 23.14 / 26.37  |
| 3 mock servers with media | 31.5 -> 29.8 | 31.4 / 59.17 -> 33.31 / 66.54   |
| 8 cameras at 1920×576     | 10.4 -> 12.4 | 97.15 / 104.05 -> 79.72 / 91.95 |

The large rig ran faster with blending forced on because its extra GPU work raised the clock from P8 to P5; nearest stayed at P8.

Changed 2026-10-18: the weight-pass timing no longer counts the depth upload that the driver defers to the texture's first draw. The earlier figure for the large rig (16.8 ms) was mostly that upload, and `'auto'` counted it as blend cost. Large rigs whose card runs at a higher clock may now keep blending.

* WebGPU against WebGL2 (8×1920×576, RTX 4090, equal clock (keeper on), one scene): the WebGPU compute path took 5.56 ms (compaction + visibility + accumulation, resolve not timed) against 3.17 ms for the WebGL2 passes. One scene, not a general ranking.
* `forceWebgl2Blend()` (**Blend anyway**) forces it on.

Two differences from WebGPU remain:

* **Border band.** WebGL2 drops a dot whose centre is just outside the view, where WebGPU clips it pixel by pixel. So a band up to half a dot wide at the edge of the view can differ: 1 pixel at the default 2-pixel dots, up to 32 pixels at the largest 64-pixel dots. The same happens at the camera's near plane, 1 cm in front of the camera.
* **Scene depth.** As on WebGPU, the blended cloud does not hide the grid or the placement gizmo behind it. With plain WebGL2 dots it does.

To compare it with WebGPU yourself, see the render check's `blend=webgl2` in [Test the client](/docs/client/developer/test-the-client).

## Connection timing [#connection-timing]

`ServerConnectionOptions.timing` (`client/src/connections/serverConnection.ts`).

### Reconnect policy [#reconnect-policy]

`DEFAULT_RECONNECT_POLICY`, in `timing.reconnect`:

| Option            | Default | Meaning                                                                                             |
| ----------------- | ------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `enabled`         | `true`  | Reconnect after a session ends, except after a local close or a protocol version mismatch           |
| `initialDelayUs`  | 1 s     | Wait before the first attempt                                                                       |
| `backoffFactor`   | 2       | Each further attempt waits this many times longer                                                   |
| `maxDelayUs`      | 30 s    | Longest wait                                                                                        |
