# View in VR (https://irc-hslu.github.io/orbbecstreamer/docs/client/view-in-vr)



Headset viewing is experimental. It is off by default in the package. It does not work out of the box: you turn it on yourself, and the headset must open the viewer over HTTPS with a trusted certificate.

The team has not yet tried this on a headset; it has been checked only in an emulator. Treat it as a test build.

## What you need [#what-you-need]

* A server PC with LAN viewers turned on. They use HTTPS on port 8443. See [Remote viewers on the LAN](/docs/getting-started/install-package#remote-viewers-on-the-lan).
* A headset that the page can reach on the LAN: Apple Vision Pro or Meta Quest 3 / 3S.
* The headset's browser must support WebXR, the browser API for headsets, and must trust the server's certificate.

## Turn it on [#turn-it-on]

1. Set up LAN viewers on the server PC, as the install page says.
2. Trust the installation's certificate authority on the headset. Use the same fingerprint check as step 4 of [Remote viewers on the LAN](/docs/getting-started/install-package#remote-viewers-on-the-lan): the fingerprint on the headset must match the one on the server PC. How to import a certificate differs by headset. The team has not tried it on either.
3. In the headset's browser, open `https://<server-hostname>.local:8443/?xr=1` or `https://<server-LAN-IP>:8443/?xr=1`. The name or address must be one the server's certificate covers.

`?xr=1` is the only switch for users. Without it the client loads nothing for VR.

## Enter VR [#enter-vr]

With `?xr=1`, in a browser that has WebXR, an **Enter VR** button appears next to the side-panel toggle. Without WebXR there is no button. If VR can't start, the button is disabled and its tip says why, for example `VR is not available in this browser` or `VR needs the 3D view`.

With the flag on, the client draws with WebGL2, because the 3D engine presents VR only on WebGL2.

Select **Enter VR**. Inside the headset you see the point clouds and a small status pill, for example `● 2 of 2 Streaming`. The pill names a problem when one server is **Delayed** or **Stale**.

## Use the panel [#use-the-panel]

Select the pill to open the panel. Select **Close**, or press B or Y on a Quest controller, to close it. The panel has three tabs: **Servers**, **View** and **Place**.

* **Servers** lists each server with its state and capture-to-display time. At the bottom are **Seated** and **Larger text**, and **Exit VR**.
* **View** has **Point size**, **Shape** (**Square** or **Round**) and **Snap turn**.
* **Place** has **Life size**, **Tabletop**, **Recentre**, and **Turn**, **Scale** and **Height** controls.

Not built yet: the **Notices** list, a comfort vignette, and markers for world anchors and cameras. The panel does not show controls for them.

## Move the scene [#move-the-scene]

* **Grab:** press and hold on empty space to hold the scene, then move your hand to move it.
* **Scale and turn:** hold with both hands. Moving them apart or together scales the scene. Turning the line between them turns it.
* **Snap turn:** on Meta Quest 3 / 3S, push the right stick sideways to turn by 30° (45° can be chosen with **Snap turn** in **View**). On Apple Vision Pro there is no stick: use **Snap turn** in the **View** tab.
* **Seated:** use it when you sit. It lowers the floor to a seated eye height.
* **Larger text:** makes the panel text larger. The panel pages instead of growing.

Expected on Apple Vision Pro (not yet seen on a device): the points fade out near the edge of the play area, and the session ends if you stay outside. The notice reads `Near the edge of the play area`.

## Leave VR [#leave-vr]

Select **Exit VR** in the panel, or use the headset's own exit. The desktop page shows `Left VR`.

## Device notes [#device-notes]

* **Apple Vision Pro:** gaze and pinch. No stick, so use the panel for snap turn.
* **Meta Quest 3 / 3S:** controllers or hands. Right-stick snap turn.

## Troubleshooting [#troubleshooting]

* **The page says the connection is not private:** the headset does not trust the certificate. Repeat step 2.
* **The `.local` name doesn't open on the headset:** use the server's LAN IP address instead, if the certificate covers it. Whether the Quest resolves `.local` names is untested.
* **No Enter VR button:** check that the URL has `?xr=1` and that the headset's browser supports WebXR.
* **`VR needs a reload to start. Reload now?`:** accept. The client reloads once to switch to WebGL2.
* **`VR was not allowed. Allow it in the browser's site settings, then try again.`:** allow VR for the site.
* **`VR ended: you left the play area. Enter VR again.`:** select **Enter VR** again.

More about the flag for developers, including the development server: [Runtime options](/docs/client/developer/runtime-options#enter-vr-experimental-behind-a-flag).


# Move around the 3D view (https://irc-hslu.github.io/orbbecstreamer/docs/client/viewer)









The 3D view fills the window behind the side panel and draws one coloured point cloud per bundle for every connected server and open recording, in one shared scene. Each point is one depth pixel, coloured by the same pixel of the colour video, and each cloud sits where its server’s placement puts it.

Today the 3D view stays empty in the main client, because no browser tested so far decodes HEVC video. You can still move the camera, and the placement handle appears in the view. See [Check your browser](/docs/client/browser-requirements).

## Move the camera [#move-the-camera]

1. Connect a server or play a recording. The clouds appear as soon as decoded frames arrive; there is nothing to switch on.
2. Click the 3D view once, or press **Tab** until it shows a focus ring, so that it receives your key presses. Screen readers call it the **3D view**.
3. Move around with the controls in this table. To see the 3D view alone, select the panel button at its top right (**Hide panel**).

| Action                        | Mouse                                                                 | Touch                 | Keyboard                    |
| ----------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------- | --------------------------- |
| Orbit around the target point | Drag with the left button                                             | Drag with one finger  | Arrow keys                  |
| Pan (move the target point)   | Drag with the right button, or **Ctrl** and drag with the left button | Drag with two fingers | **Ctrl** and arrow keys     |
| Zoom in and out               | Mouse wheel                                                           | Pinch                 | **Alt+Up** and **Alt+Down** |

The camera turns around a target point that starts 2 metres in front of the scene origin. At start, the camera sits 3 metres from that point, slightly above it, looking forward.

Each wheel step zooms by about 2 % of the current distance, so zooming is fine up close and fast far away. Points closer than 1 cm or farther than 100 metres from the camera aren’t drawn. There is no reset button: to get back to the start view, move back by hand.

## What you should see [#what-you-should-see]

Once your browser decodes a server’s video, you should see a coloured point cloud on a dark background. Gaps appear where the depth reading was missing or out of range; the view hides those pixels instead of drawing them at the near or far limit. Until then, the view is dark and empty.

The range comes from each server’s depth calibration, so a near-range server works too: one calibrated for 200 mm to 5 m draws points from 20 cm in front of its cameras.

The following picture doesn’t come from the main client. It shows what the renderer draws with WebGL2, using the synthetic two-camera scene of the developer render check.

<img alt="A point cloud of a checkerboard wall with an orange sphere in front of it, and a gap in the wall behind the sphere. This is test data drawn by the client’s renderer on a test page, because the capture browser couldn’t decode HEVC video" src="__img0" />

When frames are drawn, the card’s **Pairs** keeps going up, and its bundle rows under **Details** read `ready, drawing`.

The view redraws only when something changes: a new frame, a camera move, a setting or a window resize. While nothing changes, it draws nothing and leaves the GPU idle.

Each point is a square dot 2 device pixels wide, with WebGPU and with WebGL2. On a display scaled to 200 %, a dot looks 1 pixel wide. The view stays sharp when you resize the panel or window, or move the window to a screen with another scaling. The **WebGPU** or **WebGL2** chip in the header says which backend is in use. See [Check your browser](/docs/client/browser-requirements).

Where two cameras see the same surface, the view blends their colours instead of mixing their dots. See [Blend overlapping cameras](#blend-overlapping-cameras).

These viewer features are coming soon:

* A control to change the point size, points that grow when you get closer, and round points
* Headset viewing. It is experimental and off by default. See [View in VR](/docs/client/view-in-vr).

The view has no switches for colour only, depth only or the foreground mask. These are not planned yet.

### When the tab is in the background [#when-the-tab-is-in-the-background]

After the client's tab has been hidden for 10 s, the client stops receiving and decoding streams, recordings included. Connections and a held setup lock stay up: the client renews the lock from a timer that the browser doesn't slow down in background tabs, as long as the browser keeps the tab running. While it holds a setup lock, the client also holds a Web Lock, which keeps Chrome from freezing the tab (for example with Energy Saver, or when a background tab uses a lot of CPU). Chrome can still discard the tab when the computer runs low on memory, and other browsers may freeze it anyway: a discarded or frozen tab stops renewing, and the lock runs out 15 s later. While a headset (WebXR) session runs, streams never pause.

Once the server has accepted the pause, each point cloud leaves the 3D view, so a frozen picture is never shown as live. When you come back, streams restart at once and each bundle's cloud returns at the server's next keyframe: usually well under a second, at most one keyframe interval. A recording continues from where it would be in real time, not from where it paused. Bundles you turned off, or that the client can't show, stay off.

## Blend overlapping cameras [#blend-overlapping-cameras]

When two or more cameras see the same surface, each of them contributes points there. Without blending, the dot nearest to you wins pixel by pixel, so the overlap looks like a noisy mix of both cameras’ colours. With blending, the view mixes the cameras’ colours smoothly, in linear light, so mixed areas keep their brightness. A camera counts more where it sees the surface well:

* it looks at the surface from close to your viewing direction;
* the surface is close to it and faces it;
* the point is away from the edge of what the camera sees, such as a silhouette or the image border, where depth readings are least reliable.

Only surfaces within a few centimetres of the nearest surface blend; a surface behind it stays hidden.

Blending works with WebGPU and, on most graphics cards, with WebGL2. With WebGL2 it looks the same as with WebGPU, with two small differences:

* **Border band.** A dot whose centre is just outside the view is dropped whole, so a band up to half a dot wide at the edge of the view can differ: 1 pixel at the default 2-pixel dots.
* **No scene depth.** As with WebGPU, the blended cloud doesn't hide the grid or the placement handles behind it. Plain WebGL2 dots do.

In a headset (WebXR), the nearest dot always wins for now.

The following pictures don’t come from the main client. They show the renderer on a developer test page, with test data from two cameras whose colours are tinted red and blue so that their overlap stands out. Without blending, the overlap is a noise of red and blue dots:

<img alt="Point cloud of a checkerboard wall with a sphere in front, drawn without blending: where the two cameras overlap, the squares are a speckled mix of red-tinted and blue-tinted dots" src="__img1" />

With blending, the colours mix smoothly, and each camera fades out towards its own edges, such as around the sphere’s shadow on the wall:

<img alt="The same scene drawn with blending: the squares are evenly coloured, with smooth red-to-blue transitions where one camera’s view ends" src="__img2" />

### Switch blending on or off [#switch-blending-on-or-off]

Blending is on by default.

1. Find the **View** section under the header of the side panel.
2. Turn the **Blend** switch on or off. The view changes at once.
3. Read the line under the switch. It says how points are drawn now:

| Status line                                                                                                   | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Blending overlapping cameras.`                                                                               | Blending is on.                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| `Blending off: the nearest point is drawn.`                                                                   | You switched blending off.                                                                                                                                                                      |
| `Preparing blending… plain points meanwhile.`                                                                 | The graphics card is still preparing blending, for a moment after the page loads. Plain dots are drawn meanwhile.                                                                               |
| `Blending unavailable, plain points: …` or `Blending unavailable, nearest point drawn: …`                     | The graphics card couldn’t run blending, for example `16-bit float targets unavailable`. The text after the colon says why. Plain dots are drawn.                                               |
| `Nearest point drawn. …`                                                                                      | Blending was turned off automatically; the rest says why. See [When blending turns itself off](#when-blending-turns-itself-off).                                                                |
| `Checking the blending cost… nearest point meanwhile.` or `Blending overlapping cameras (checking its cost).` | WebGL2 only, when the browser hides the graphics card's name or can't time the GPU: for about 2 seconds of drawing after the page loads, the client checks that blending doesn't slow the view. |
| `Blending overlapping cameras (forced on).`                                                                   | You selected **Blend anyway**.                                                                                                                                                                  |

The settings stay in this browser tab only. They aren’t sent to any server, and they go back to the defaults when you reload the page.

### When blending turns itself off [#when-blending-turns-itself-off]

With WebGL2, the client turns blending off by itself when it would make the view slow:

| Status line ends with                                              | Why                                                                                                                |                                                                                                                                                                    |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `SwiftShader: blending off by default.`                            | The browser draws in software, without the graphics card.                                                          | Blending would make the view very slow.                                                                                                                            |
| `Blending off: over 40 % of the frame budget (… of … ms).`         | Blending took more than 40 % of each frame for 2 seconds.                                                          | The numbers are the blending time and the frame time. The frame time counts as at least 1/60 s, so a fast screen (120 or 144 Hz) doesn't turn blending off sooner. |
| `Blending off: it slowed frames by … ms at start-up (limit … ms).` | The browser hides the graphics card's name, or can't time the GPU, and the start-up check found blending too slow. |                                                                                                                                                                    |

**What blending costs with WebGL2, and when big rigs fall back:**

* Blending times itself while the view runs, so it sees the clock the graphics card really uses. A card on a light scene often stays at its idle clock, and blending costs more there.
* On a strong graphics card, 1 or 2 cameras blend at no visible cost, even at the idle clock.
* Around 4 cameras, blending takes about 2.7 ms of GPU time per frame at the idle clock (under the 6.7 ms limit), and about 14 % of the frame rate (50 to 43 frames per second).
* Large rigs, such as 8 cameras at 1920×576, take about 12 ms per frame at the idle clock and fall back to the nearest dot automatically, after 2 seconds. At full clock the same rig takes about 3 ms and keeps blending. Weaker graphics cards are expected to fall back with fewer cameras (not measured).
* **Blend anyway** forces blending on.

Measured 2026-10-18 (operator freeze 10:03-10:35 UTC) on synthetic scenes, NVIDIA RTX 4090 only (Chrome for Testing 155), 3 runs, medians; an unrelated background job was present but idle. "Idle clock": the card chose its own clock (mostly P8, 210 MHz). "Full clock": a separate GPU load held the card at P2 (2670 MHz) and shared the GPU with the view.

Plain dots are drawn instead. To blend anyway:

1. In the **View** section, select **Blend anyway** under the status line.
2. Blending stays on until you reload the page, even if it slows the view.

Switching **Blend** off and on again also runs the check again, except with software drawing (SwiftShader): there, use **Blend anyway**.

### Tune blending [#tune-blending]

Open **Blend tuning** in the **View** section to change how cameras are weighed. [What you can tweak](/docs/client/what-you-can-tweak#blend-tuning) lists the eight fields, their ranges and defaults, and when to change each. **Reset tuning** restores every default.

## Change how dots look [#change-how-dots-look]

Open **Points** in the **View** section to change the dot size, switch between screen-sized and scene-sized dots (**Size mode**), and choose square or round dots (**Shape**). These work with both WebGPU and WebGL2, and the view changes at once. [What you can tweak](/docs/client/what-you-can-tweak#points) lists every field, its range and its default. **Reset points** restores the defaults. The settings stay in this browser tab only.

## Fix drawing problems [#fix-drawing-problems]

| What you see                                                                           | Why                                                                                                                                                     | What to do                                                                                                                                            |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| The header shows a red **No 3D view** chip                                             | The browser has neither WebGPU nor WebGL2, or hardware acceleration is off.                                                                             | Turn on hardware acceleration, or try another browser. See [Check your browser](/docs/client/browser-requirements).                                   |
| The card shows a **Setup and control only** chip                                       | The browser can’t decode the video, so there are no frames to draw.                                                                                     | Use a browser and machine with HEVC decoding.                                                                                                         |
| **Pairs** stays at 0, and the bundle row under **Details** stays `ready, no frame yet` | No frames reach the client.                                                                                                                             | Check that the server is streaming. The card’s status chip and `last close` box say whether the connection is up.                                     |
| **Pairs** and **Dropped** go up, but **uploaded** under **Details** doesn’t            | Frames arrive but belong to a newer server setup than the one the client holds.                                                                         | Wait: the client fetches the new setup and resumes by itself. If it doesn’t, select **Remove** on the card and add the server again.                  |
| The cloud freezes or disappears for a moment after a calibration or placement change   | The client never draws a frame with the setup of another revision.                                                                                      | Wait. Drawing resumes once the new setup arrives.                                                                                                     |
| A bundle row under **Details** shows `upload error: …`                                 | The graphics card rejected a frame. The bundle stays hidden until the next good frame.                                                                  | This usually clears by itself. If it keeps happening, reload the page.                                                                                |
| The clouds disappear after the graphics driver or GPU resets                           | The browser lost its GPU device.                                                                                                                        | Wait: the clouds come back by themselves within a few frames. If they don’t, reload the page.                                                         |
| One bundle isn’t blended with the others, while blending is on                         | Its points don’t fit the GPU’s buffer limit: about 5.6 million depth pixels per bundle on a GPU that allows no more. The bundle is drawn as plain dots. | Configure the server with fewer or smaller cameras per bundle, for example one bundle per camera.                                                     |
| A bundle row under **Details** shows `rendering incompatible (too-many-tiles): …`      | The bundle packs more than 16 cameras into one stream.                                                                                                  | Configure the server with 16 cameras or fewer per bundle, for example one bundle per camera.                                                          |
| A bundle row under **Details** shows `metadata invalid (…)`                            | The server’s description of this bundle doesn’t add up. The client keeps the last good frame.                                                           | Check the server’s calibration and placement.                                                                                                         |
| The cloud looks mirrored, left to right or top to bottom                               | The server sent its camera poses without converting them to the protocol's frame. Recordings made before that fix carry the old poses.                  | Report it with the server version and its calibration.                                                                                                |
| Two servers’ clouds overlap                                                            | Their placements put them in the same place.                                                                                                            | [Place a server in the scene](/docs/client/placement-editing), or [move an anchor in your view](/docs/client/world-anchors).                          |
| A cloud moved in your view but not for other people                                    | You moved its anchor, or you have an uncommitted placement draft. Both stay in your browser.                                                            | Commit the placement, or select **Reset** on the anchor or **Discard** on the draft.                                                                  |
| The picture tears with WebGL2, showing parts of two frames                             | The client asks WebGL2 for a low-latency canvas, which can tear.                                                                                        | This is expected: it trades tearing for lower delay.                                                                                                  |
| The view is slow or jerky                                                              | Each camera adds about one point per depth pixel.                                                                                                       | Close other graphics-heavy tabs, and connect only the servers you need. Turn **Blend** off in the **View** section: blending draws every point twice. |
| The **View** status line says `Blending unavailable, plain points: …`                  | The graphics card or driver couldn’t run blending. The view falls back to plain dots.                                                                   | Reload the page. If it stays, update the graphics driver, and report the text after the colon.                                                        |
| A surface shows through another one in front of it                                     | The depth tolerance is larger than the gap between the two surfaces.                                                                                    | Lower **Depth tolerance (m)** or **Depth tolerance per metre** under **Blend tuning**.                                                                |
| Where cameras overlap, the colours look smeared or doubled                             | The cameras’ placements or calibrations don’t quite agree, so blending mixes two slightly shifted images.                                               | Check the placements and calibrations. Meanwhile, raise **View-angle sharpness**, so that one camera dominates.                                       |
| Where cameras overlap, the surface is speckled even with blending on                   | The two cameras see the surface more than the depth tolerance apart, so only the nearer one is drawn at each pixel.                                     | Raise **Depth tolerance (m)** a little, or check the cameras’ calibration.                                                                            |


# What you can tweak (https://irc-hslu.github.io/orbbecstreamer/docs/client/what-you-can-tweak)













Every control in the client, one table per area; [Tour of the client](/docs/client/tour) shows where the areas are. Unless a row says otherwise, a change applies at once and lasts until you reload the page.

An unavailable button stays visible. Hover over it, or focus it with the keyboard, to see why:

<img alt="A tip over the server card’s release-lock button: Release lock, This client does not hold the lock" src="__img0" />

## Window and theme [#window-and-theme]

| Control                                                                  | What it changes                                                                               | Default | When to change it             |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------- | ----------------------------- |
| Panel toggle, top right of the 3D view (**Hide panel** / **Show panel**) | Hides the side panel, so the 3D view fills the window                                         | Shown   | To look at the scene alone    |
| Sun or moon button in the header (**Light theme** / **Dark theme**)      | The panel’s theme. This browser remembers it. The 3D view stays dark.                         | Dark    | In a bright room              |
| **i** next to the header chips                                           | Shows the renderer notes, for example why WebGL2 was picked. Only shown when there are notes. |         | When the chip says **WebGL2** |

## View section [#view-section]

<img alt="The View section: the Blend switch on, the status line Blending overlapping cameras., Points open with its five settings and Reset points, and Blend tuning open with its eight fields at their defaults and Reset tuning" src="__img1" />

| Control          | What it changes                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                | Default | When to change it                                                    |
| ---------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Blend**        | On: where cameras overlap, their colours mix smoothly. Off: the dot nearest to you wins. Works with WebGPU and, where the graphics card can, with WebGL2; otherwise the switch is off and unavailable.                                                                                                                                                                                         | On      | Turn it off when the view is slow: blending draws every point twice. |
| **Blend anyway** | Shown with WebGL2 when the client turned blending off by itself (software drawing, or too slow). Turns it back on until you reload the page. See [When blending turns itself off](/docs/client/viewer#when-blending-turns-itself-off).                                                                                                                                                         |         | When you want blending even if the view gets slower                  |
| **Show floor**   | On: draws a ground grid at the scene’s floor level, and each server’s measured floor as a translucent square under its cloud. Off: neither. It is a setting of this browser only; the client remembers it. Servers without a measured floor draw no square. When the squares and the grid don’t line up, the floor isn’t aligned yet: see [Calibrate the floor](/docs/client/calibrate-floor). | Off     | When you set up or check a server’s floor                            |
| **Reset tuning** | Sets the eight **Blend tuning** fields below back to their defaults. **Blend** stays as it is.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |         | After experimenting                                                  |

### Points [#points]

Open **Points** for how each dot is drawn. These settings work with both WebGPU and WebGL2, and change the view at once. With WebGL2, some graphics cards can't draw dots as large as 64 pixels; there, large dots stay smaller than the value you set. Type a value, then press **Enter** or leave the field; a value out of range is set to the nearest allowed one.

| Control             | What it does                                                                                                                  | Range           | Default | When to change it                                   |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------- | ------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| **Size mode**       | **Screen**: every dot has the same size on screen. **World**: dots are sized like the scene, so they grow as you move closer. | Screen or World | Screen  | Choose World when gaps open between dots up close   |
| **Point size (px)** | The size of every dot in screen mode. Unavailable in World mode.                                                              | 1 to 64         | 2       | Raise it to fill gaps; lower it for fine detail     |
| **World scale**     | In World mode, how many depth pixels wide each dot is. Above 1, neighbours overlap. Unavailable in Screen mode.               | 0 or more       | 1.5     | Raise it when gaps show on slanted surfaces         |
| **Max size (px)**   | In World mode, the largest a dot may get when you are close. Unavailable in Screen mode.                                      | 1 to 64         | 16      | Lower it when the view gets slow close to a surface |
| **Shape**           | **Square** or **Round** dots                                                                                                  | Square or Round | Square  | Round looks softer; square is the fastest           |
| **Reset points**    | Sets the five settings above back to their defaults                                                                           |                 |         | After experimenting                                 |

Sizes are in screen pixels of the drawn picture. At 200 % display scaling, 2 px is one CSS pixel. The settings stay in this browser tab only and go back to the defaults when you reload the page.

### Blend tuning [#blend-tuning]

Open **Blend tuning** for eight fields; hover over a field for its one-line hint. Type a value, then press **Enter** or leave the field. A value out of range is set to the nearest allowed one. The fields are unavailable while **Blend** is off.

| Field                         | What raising it does                                                                         | Range          | Default | When to change it                                                                        |
| ----------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------- | ------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **View-angle sharpness**      | Favours the camera whose view is closest to yours. At 0, the view angle doesn’t matter.      | 0 to 64        | 4       | Overlaps look smeared or doubled                                                         |
| **Depth tolerance (m)**       | Blends surfaces farther apart in depth instead of hiding one                                 | 0 or more      | 0.01    | Lower it when a surface shows through one in front; raise it when overlaps stay speckled |
| **Depth tolerance per metre** | Adds tolerance per metre of distance from you                                                | 0 or more      | 0.01    | Scenes far from the cameras                                                              |
| **Edge fade width (px)**      | Fades a camera out over more depth pixels at the edges of what it sees. Whole numbers.       | 1 to 16        | 8       | Seams along object edges                                                                 |
| **Edge step (per m)**         | Needs a bigger depth jump, times the distance, to count as an edge: 2.5 cm at 1 m by default | 0.0001 or more | 0.025   | Sloped surfaces fade as if they were edges                                               |
| **Full-weight distance (m)**  | Points up to this distance from their camera count fully; farther ones count less            | 0.001 or more  | 1       | Cameras sit farther than 1 m from the subject                                            |
| **Grazing-angle floor**       | Raises the lowest weight of surfaces seen edge-on                                            | 0 to 1         | 0.1     | Edge-on surfaces drop out of the blend                                                   |
| **Splat falloff**             | Makes each dot count less towards its rim                                                    | 0 to 64        | 2       | Mixing between neighbouring dots looks rough                                             |

| Lock icon (**Acquire lock**)           | Takes the setup lock without opening setup                                                 | To keep others from changing the server           |
| Open-lock icon (**Release lock**)      | Gives the lock back                                                                        | When you’re done holding it                       |

## Setup view [#setup-view]

| Control                                                | What it does                                                                                 | When to use it                                          |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Leave**                                              | Cancels a running calibration, releases the lock, closes setup. Commits nothing.             | When you’re done. Commit first what you want to keep.   |
| **Enter setup**, **Back**                              | Ask for the lock again, or close setup, after the session ended                              | After you were forced out                               |
| **Start**, **Cancel**, **Commit** (Depth quantization) | Run, stop, or put a depth calibration in force                                               | See [Calibrate depth](/docs/client/calibration)         |
| **Calibrate floor**, **Commit**, **Cancel** (Floor)    | Measure, keep or throw away the floor. Only shown when the server offers it.                 | See [Calibrate the floor](/docs/client/calibrate-floor) |
| **Level to floor** (Floor)                             | Opens a placement draft that levels the cloud to the measured floor. Commit it in Placement. | After the floor is measured                             |
| **Log** / **Linear** (Depth codes)                     | The histogram’s scale. Default **Log**.                                                      | **Linear** to compare the big peaks                     |

## Placement [#placement]

| Control                                         | What it changes                                                                           | Range and default                                 | When to change it               |
| ----------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| **Edit**                                        | Starts a draft equal to the server’s placement                                            |                                                   | To move the server              |
| **x (m)**, **y (m)**, **z (m)**                 | Position relative to the anchor. +X right, +Y up, +Z forward.                             | −1000 to 1000 m, shown to 1 mm                    | Exact position                  |
| **yaw (°)**, **pitch (°)**, **roll (°)**        | Rotation, roll first, then pitch, then yaw                                                | −360 to 360°, shown to 0.1° with pitch −90 to 90° | Exact rotation                  |
| **−** / **+**, or **Arrow Down** / **Arrow Up** | Steps a field by 0.01 m or 1°; **Shift** with the arrow keys steps ten times that         |                                                   | Nudging                         |

| **Commit**                                      | Sends the draft; every client then draws the server there                                 |                                                   | The draft is right              |
| **Rebase**                                      | Keeps your pose on a newer server placement. Shown when someone else committed meanwhile. |                                                   | Before committing a stale draft |
| **Discard**                                     | Drops the draft                                                                           |                                                   | To start over                   |

## World anchors [#world-anchors]

| Control                             | What it changes                                                                                        | Default              | When to change it                   |
| ----------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| **x (m)** … **roll (°)** per anchor | Where this browser draws the anchor and its servers. Never sent to a server. Same fields as placement. | At the origin, all 0 | To line servers up in your own view |
| **Reset**                           | Puts the anchor back at the origin                                                                     |                      | To undo your changes                |

## 3D view [#3d-view]

No settings; [Move around the 3D view](/docs/client/viewer#move-the-camera) lists the camera controls:

* **Orbit**: drag with the left button, or the arrow keys
* **Pan**: drag with the right button, or **Ctrl** with the arrow keys
* **Zoom**: the mouse wheel, or **Alt+Up** and **Alt+Down**

## What you can’t change in the client [#what-you-cant-change-in-the-client]

* **Point size and shape**: square dots 2 device pixels wide. Other sizes, round dots and a debug view are [developer options](/docs/client/developer/developer-options#point-settings).
* **Playback speed, looping and seeking**: set by the recording’s manifest. See [Manifest fields](/docs/client/playback#manifest-fields).
* **Reconnect delays and timeouts**: [developer options](/docs/client/developer/developer-options#connection-timing).
* **Background pause**: streams pause after the tab is hidden for 10 s. See [When the tab is in the background](/docs/client/viewer#when-the-tab-is-in-the-background).
* **Colour-only, depth-only and mask views**: not planned yet


# Move an anchor in your view (https://irc-hslu.github.io/orbbecstreamer/docs/client/world-anchors)





Each server’s placement is relative to a named anchor, for example a marker or a corner of the room. The **World anchors** section decides where each anchor sits in your 3D view. These anchor positions are remembered in this browser and restored after a reload (**Reset** forgets one). They stay in this browser: the client never sends them to a server, and they never change a server’s placement.

To change where a server sits for everyone, see [Place a server in the scene](/docs/client/placement-editing) instead.

## Move an anchor [#move-an-anchor]

1. Connect a server. **World anchors**, below the server cards, lists every anchor a connected server names. No lock needed.
2. Find the anchor by name, for example **anchor-dev**. The line under it lists its servers and reads `at origin`, or `custom pose` once you moved it.
3. Type in **x (m)**, **y (m)**, **z (m)**, **yaw (°)**, **pitch (°)** or **roll (°)**. A valid value applies at once, and the anchor’s servers move with it in your 3D view. The fields work like the [placement fields](/docs/client/placement-editing#edit-the-draft-with-numbers).
4. To put the anchor back at the origin, select **Reset**.

<img alt="World anchors with one anchor, anchor-dev, used by the Dev mock server at origin: the Anchor pose (this browser only) fields, all zero, and Reset" src="__img0" />

Other people’s views don’t change. The section is hidden while the setup view is open.

## Fix anchor problems [#fix-anchor-problems]

* **`No connected server names an anchor yet.`**: no server is connected, or the connected servers have no placement yet. Connect a server and wait until its card shows **Ready** or **Streaming**.
* **`Not applied (not a rigid transform): …`**: the client refused a pose that would stretch or mirror the scene, and nothing changed. The fields can’t produce such a pose, so this is a bug. Report it with the values you typed.
* **The anchors are back at the origin after a reload**: the browser blocked or cleared its site storage (private window, cleared data), so nothing was remembered. Set them again.
* **A server moved for you but not for anyone else**: this is how anchors work. To move a server for everyone, [place it in the scene](/docs/client/placement-editing).


# First stream (https://irc-hslu.github.io/orbbecstreamer/docs/getting-started/first-stream)



<Callout type="warn">
  Live video in the browser needs v0.1.0-poc.7 or later. With poc.6 and
  earlier, a browser gets the server's status and setup but no video; use
  the server's telemetry and debug recordings (below) to see your capture.
  Up to v0.1.4 the team has checked the depth picture on a live scene once,
  on a development build in a dark room. It has not yet checked the colour
  picture or depth calibration on a live, lit scene on real hardware.
</Callout>

## Connect a browser to the release package [#connect-a-browser-to-the-release-package]

With the [release package](/docs/getting-started/install-package) installed
and at least one Orbbec camera connected:

1. Make sure the server runs. From v0.1.0-poc.10 the install starts it,
   with the cameras closed. Up to poc.9, start it yourself:

   ```bash
   sudo systemctl start orbbec-streamer
   ```

   Up to poc.8, the gateway starts only once a camera is active.

2. In Chrome or Edge **on the server PC**, open
   [http://127.0.0.1:8080](http://127.0.0.1:8080) (or
   `http://localhost:8080`). By default the gateway accepts only these two
   page addresses; for other computers, see
   [Remote viewers on the LAN](/docs/getting-started/install-package#remote-viewers-on-the-lan).

3. The client finds the server by itself and adds it; you type nothing. A
   server card appears under **Servers**.

4. From v0.1.0-poc.9 the card reads **Cameras closed**: select **Start
   cameras**. Opening the cameras can take up to a minute.

**Expected result:** the card connects and shows the server's state and
calibration chips. From poc.7, with one camera, the point cloud appears: the
server writes the camera's identity pose at its first start, so there is no
setup step. Several cameras need a camera-pose calibration with a ChArUco
board first, which the team has not yet validated on hardware (from
v0.1.0-poc.11 in the Operator Console, see
[Calibrate the camera poses](/docs/operator#calibrate-the-camera-poses); up to
poc.10 see [Camera pose calibration](/docs/server/camera-calibration)); until then the
card shows the server needs setup and no point cloud. How much CPU the
decoder needs depends on the PC; see
[Check your browser](/docs/client/browser-requirements). If the card shows **Server
or camera not running**, start the server as in step 1 and connect a
camera; the card then connects by itself. For other problems, and for
typing the address and certificate hash by hand, see
[Add a server](/docs/client/add-a-server).

The [Operator Console](/docs/operator) at
`http://127.0.0.1:8080/operator` connects the same way. From poc.7 its
**Preview** screen shows the same live video.

## Run a source build on your own cameras [#run-a-source-build-on-your-own-cameras]

This needs a [server built from source](/docs/getting-started/install-server)
and at least one attached Orbbec camera.

<Steps>
  <Step>
    ## Adapt the config to your rig [#adapt-the-config-to-your-rig]

    `config/dev/live.yaml` describes the development rig, not yours. Copy it and
    edit the camera serial numbers, sync settings and mask backend for your own
    cameras. Full steps:
    [Adapt the config to your rig](/docs/server/running#adapt-the-config-to-your-rig).

    The short version, from `server/`:

    ```bash
    mkdir -p config/local
    cp config/dev/live.yaml config/local/live.yaml
    ./build/dev-debug/orbbec_streamer --orbbec-test   # read each camera's serial
    ```

    Then edit `config/local/live.yaml`: set each camera's `serial_number`, and
    either build the RVM engine or set `mask.backend: fill_all` to run without
    segmentation.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ## Run it [#run-it]

    ```bash
    cd server
    ./build/dev-debug/orbbec_streamer --live config/local/live.yaml
    ```
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ## Watch it work [#watch-it-work]

    The terminal redraws a rate table roughly every 5 seconds. After the
    warm-up, every stage should reach your configured frame rate with 0 drops.
    See [Read the telemetry](/docs/server/telemetry) for what each line means,
    and [Run the server](/docs/server/running#expected-result) for a full
    worked log.

    Stop it with `Ctrl+C` when you're done; it shuts down cleanly.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ## Watch your own capture [#watch-your-own-capture]

    With `debug_recording.record_gpu_outputs: true` and
    `locally_decode_gpu_outputs: true` in the config, open
    `debug/live/<camera>/gpu-output-depth-inferno.mkv` in any video player to
    see your own depth stream, colourised. See
    [Run the server](/docs/server/running#debug-recording-output) for the full
    file list.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ## Optional: preview it in the client [#optional-preview-it-in-the-client]

    The browser client can also play back the server's debug recording, without
    a server. The server writes `manifest.json` at the top of `debug/live/` (from
    v0.1.0-poc.6), and from v0.1.0-poc.7 the client opens that folder. In the
    client, unfold **Open recording** under **Servers**, choose that folder (the one that holds `manifest.json`, not single files) under
    **Recording folder (with manifest.json)**, or use **Browse for the folder…**,
    then select **Play recording**. With an older server there is no manifest:
    you write one by hand alongside the raw `.hevc` files. See
    [Play a recording](/docs/client/playback) for the steps and the manifest
    format. Desktop Chrome plays a recording, also on a Linux PC with an NVIDIA
    GPU, where the client uses its built-in WebAssembly decoder; see
    [Check your browser](/docs/client/browser-requirements).
  </Step>
</Steps>

## Troubleshooting [#troubleshooting]

Every start-up failure and its fix are in
[Run the server](/docs/server/running#troubleshooting) and
[Configuration](/docs/server/configuration#troubleshooting). For calibrating
depth quantization or camera pose next, see
[Calibration](/docs/guides/calibration).


# Install the release package (https://irc-hslu.github.io/orbbecstreamer/docs/getting-started/install-package)



The release package installs the server, the browser client and the
[Operator Console](/docs/operator) on one Ubuntu PC, as systemd services.
Nothing is built from source. To build from source instead, see
[Build the server from source](/docs/getting-started/install-server).

<Callout type="warn">
  v0.1.0 was the first complete release: install, start the cameras,
  calibrate and view in a browser. v0.1.1 adds network sensing; v0.1.2 fills in the media rate on the Network page and fixes from the live run; v0.1.3 adds a hardware check, the WebGL2 fallback notice and console discovery, and fixes mirrored camera poses; v0.1.4 changes the default calibration board and draws it on the **Camera pose** screen, with a download to print, and blends overlapping cameras with WebGL2 where it works well; v0.1.5 fixes certificate renewal and reinstalling. It is a non-commercial proof of concept
  (GPL-3.0 segmenter, no licence check), for evaluation only. Live video (from
  v0.1.0-poc.7): browsers on the server PC get status, setup and
  the cameras' colour and depth (see
  [Serve to browsers](/docs/server/serving)). The team has checked the depth
  picture on a live scene once, on a development build in a dark room; it
  has not yet checked the colour picture or depth calibration on a live,
  lit scene on real hardware. Browsers on other computers in the LAN can view the cameras if
  you turn that on; the team has not yet tried it from a second machine. See
  [Remote viewers on the LAN](#remote-viewers-on-the-lan). The team has not
  yet installed it on a clean machine with a GPU and cameras.
</Callout>

<Steps>
  <Step>
    ## Check your machine [#check-your-machine]

    * **Ubuntu 26.04.** The package is built against its C library and FFmpeg 8;
      other releases aren't supported yet.
    * **An NVIDIA GPU** with compute capability 7.5 or newer.
    * **The NVIDIA driver 580 or newer, installed by you**, for example
      `sudo apt install nvidia-open` from NVIDIA's apt repository, then a reboot.
      The package neither contains nor installs a driver.
    * **One or more Orbbec cameras** on USB 3. Two or more also need sync
      cables between them; see [More than one camera](#more-than-one-camera).

    <Callout type="info" title="Recommended hardware (provisional; measured on stand-ins)">
      The team tested the server on an RTX 4090. For 2 cameras it expects the
      server PC to need at least an RTX 3060-class GPU, 8 CPU cores and 16 GB of
      RAM; the team has not tested that minimum yet. From v0.1.3 the machine
      check warns when the PC is below it (see [Check the machine](#check-the-machine)).

      A computer that views the cameras needs a CPU with 4 cores and 8 threads
      at 3.0 GHz or faster, 8 GB of RAM, a GPU that supports WebGL2, a current
      Chrome or Edge, and wired 1 Gbit/s Ethernet. See
      [Minimum viewer hardware](/docs/client/browser-requirements#minimum-viewer-hardware)
      for how it was measured.
    </Callout>

    Check the driver:

    ```bash
    nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name,driver_version,compute_cap --format=csv
    ```

    **Expected result:** your GPU, a driver version of 580 or higher, and a
    compute capability of 7.5 or higher.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ## Add NVIDIA's apt repository [#add-nvidias-apt-repository]

    The package pulls the CUDA runtime and TensorRT (about 2 GB) from NVIDIA's
    repository:

    ```bash
    wget https://developer.download.nvidia.com/compute/cuda/repos/ubuntu2604/x86_64/cuda-keyring_1.1-1_all.deb
    sudo dpkg -i cuda-keyring_1.1-1_all.deb && sudo apt update
    ```
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ## Install the package [#install-the-package]

    Download `orbbec-streamer_0.1.5-1_amd64.deb` from the
    [v0.1.5 release](https://github.com/irc-hslu/orbbecstreamer/releases/tag/v0.1.5),
    together with `SHA256SUMS`, or from the release link you were given. In
    the download folder, check the file, then install it:

    ```bash
    sha256sum --check --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS
    sudo apt install ./orbbec-streamer_0.1.5-1_amd64.deb
    ```

    `sha256sum` must print `orbbec-streamer_0.1.5-1_amd64.deb: OK`. The
    release lists its SHA-256 as `1440738759927db206c152a19bfaec0cb2ab594476c3b257a7a362280f9c3ba2`.

    The release also carries the source of the segmentation model and a relink
    kit for the client's video decoder, which the decoder's LGPL licence
    requires. You don't need either to install.

    The release page is in a private repository, so only people with access to
    it can download from there. There is no public download yet.

    The package version inside the file is `0.1.5-1`. It sorts above every
    poc package, so upgrading from a poc works as usual. The install:

    * creates the system user `orbbec-streamer`, the empty group
      `orbbec-operators` (see [Terminal console](/docs/operator/terminal-console#start-and-stop-without-sudo)), the state folder
      `/var/lib/orbbec-streamer` and the TLS certificates in
      `/etc/orbbec-streamer/tls`;
    * installs the udev rules for the cameras;
    * runs the machine check (below), which only reports and never stops the
      install;
    * starts `orbbec-streamer-web` and the certificate renewal timer
      `orbbec-tls-renew.timer`;
    * from v0.1.0-poc.10, enables and starts the server service
      `orbbec-streamer` with the cameras closed. You open them from the client
      or the Operator Console with **Start cameras**. It prints:

    ```text
    orbbec-streamer: installed and started; cameras closed until an app opens them: http://127.0.0.1:8080 (Start cameras), http://127.0.0.1:8080/operator or orbbec-console
    orbbec-streamer: the first start builds the segmentation engine for this GPU (minutes); follow it with: journalctl -fu orbbec-streamer
    ```

    To stop the server and keep it off at boot:

    ```bash
    sudo systemctl disable --now orbbec-streamer
    ```

    Up to poc.9, the install doesn't start or enable `orbbec-streamer`, and
    prints `installed; cameras stay off until you run: sudo systemctl start
    orbbec-streamer`; you start it in step 5.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ## Check the machine [#check-the-machine]

    ```bash
    orbbec-streamer-preflight
    ```

    **Expected result** on a ready machine, ending with `preflight: OK` (shortened: v0.1.4 also prints the `floor-*` lines below, `tensorrt-cuda-match` and one `udev-access:` line per camera):

    ```text
    PASS  nvidia-driver                driver 580.178.04 (minimum 580)
    PASS  gpu-compute-capability       NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 sm_89 (minimum sm_75)
    PASS  driver-libraries             libcuda.so.1, libnvidia-ml.so.1 (NVML) and libnvidia-encode.so.1 (NVENC) present
    PASS  cuda-runtime                 libcudart.so.13 at /usr/local/cuda/targets/x86_64-linux/lib/libcudart.so.13 (cuda-cudart-13-4 13.4.92-1)
    PASS  tensorrt                     libnvinfer.so.11 and libnvonnxparser.so.11 present (libnvinfer11 11.3.0.99-1+cuda13.4)
    PASS  usb3:2-6                     Orbbec Femto Bolt 3D Camera (066b) negotiated 5000 Mbit/s
    PASS  udev-rules                   /usr/lib/udev/rules.d/99-orbbec-streamer.rules installed
    PASS  service-account              system user 'orbbec-streamer' exists
    preflight: OK (0 FAIL, 0 WARN)
    ```

    Every `FAIL` or `WARN` line is followed by a `fix:` line that says what to
    do. `--json` prints the same results as JSON.

    From v0.1.3 three more lines compare the PC with the recommended hardware
    above: `floor-gpu`, `floor-cpu` and `floor-ram`. Below it they print `WARN`,
    never `FAIL`, so the install goes ahead; the server may still run with
    fewer cameras. `floor-gpu` rates only GeForce GPUs (RTX 30-series xx60 or
    newer, with at least 8 GB of memory); for other GPUs it passes with `not
    classified`.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ## Wait for the first start [#wait-for-the-first-start]

    Connect the cameras. From v0.1.0-poc.10 the install has already started the
    server. Up to poc.9, start it yourself, and enable it if it should also
    start at boot:

    ```bash
    sudo systemctl start orbbec-streamer
    sudo systemctl enable orbbec-streamer
    ```

    Up to poc.8, the server then starts capturing. From v0.1.0-poc.9, it
    starts with the cameras closed (idle) and waits until a client asks it to
    open them; you do that in the next step. **The first start
    builds the segmentation engine for your GPU**, whether the cameras are open
    or not: about 3 minutes, once. Until
    it's ready, frames pass through without background removal. Follow it with:

    ```bash
    journalctl -u orbbec-streamer -f
    ```

    The engine is cached in `/var/lib/orbbec-streamer/engines` and rebuilt only
    when the GPU, TensorRT, the model or the number of cameras changes.

    In v0.1.0-poc.7 the server may stop once, about 4 minutes after its first
    start, when the engine build finishes; systemd restarts it within seconds.
    poc.8 fixes this.

    With one camera, the server writes the camera's identity pose at its first
    start, so it needs no calibration (from poc.7). Several cameras need a
    camera-pose calibration first; see [More than one camera](#more-than-one-camera).
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ## Open the client [#open-the-client]

    In Chrome or Edge **on the server PC**, open [http://127.0.0.1:8080](http://127.0.0.1:8080). The
    page finds the server and its certificate by itself, so you don't enter an
    address or trust a certificate. The certificate rotates about every 6 days
    with no action from you.

    From v0.1.0-poc.9, the server's card reads **Cameras closed** until you
    select **Start cameras**. From v0.1.0-poc.10, the Operator Console has the
    same button (see [Operator Console](/docs/operator#cameras-closed)). The server then opens the cameras, which can take
    up to a minute, and stays open until the service stops. See
    [Server card](/docs/client/server-card). To open the cameras at every
    start instead, set `start_capture_on_launch: true` under `serving:` in
    `/etc/orbbec-streamer/live.yaml` and restart the service.

    From poc.7 the page shows the cameras' point cloud once the server is
    streaming. On a Linux PC with an NVIDIA GPU the client decodes the video with
    its built-in decoder, on the CPU; how much CPU
    it needs depends on the PC (see
    [Check your browser](/docs/client/browser-requirements)).

    The Operator Console is at [http://127.0.0.1:8080/operator](http://127.0.0.1:8080/operator). See
    [Operator Console](/docs/operator).
  </Step>
</Steps>

## More than one camera [#more-than-one-camera]

The package's `/etc/orbbec-streamer/live.yaml` is set up for one camera.
Two or more cameras must be hardware-synchronised:

1. Connect the sync cables between the cameras.

2. In `/etc/orbbec-streamer/live.yaml`, give every camera an entry with its
   `serial_number` (printed on the camera). Exactly one has
   `role: "primary"`; the others have `role: "secondary"`:

   ```yaml
   cameras:
     - id: "cam0"
       vendor: "orbbec"
       serial_number: "<serial of the primary camera>"
       required: true
       role: "primary"
     - id: "cam1"
       vendor: "orbbec"
       serial_number: "<serial of the second camera>"
       required: true
       role: "secondary"
   ```

3. Turn sync on, with the values tested on two Femto Bolts:

   ```yaml
   sync:
     enabled: true
     secondary_depth_delay_step_us: 160
     trigger_out_enable: true
     timestamp_tolerance_us: 5000
   ```

4. Run `sudo systemctl restart orbbec-streamer`.

5. Calibrate the camera poses with a printed ChArUco board: the one in
   `calibration.board` of your `live.yaml`, or the default 4 × 6 board
   (see [Calibration board](#calibration-board)). From
   v0.1.0-poc.11, do it in the Operator Console; see
   [Calibrate the camera poses](/docs/operator#calibrate-the-camera-poses).
   Up to poc.10, do it on the server; see
   [Camera pose calibration](/docs/server/camera-calibration). Until then the
   server stays in “needs setup” and sends no video. The team has tested
   this calibration with synthetic cameras only, not yet on hardware. One
   camera needs no calibration (from poc.7).

See [Configuration](/docs/server/configuration#sync) for every sync key.
Without sync, the server refuses to start with several cameras:
`sync.enabled=false allows only one camera …`. (v0.1.0-poc.4 started and
then stopped after about 10 seconds with `no batch for 10005 ms: the
cameras' frame sets no longer match …`.)

## Files and services [#files-and-services]

| Path                                           | What it is                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| ---------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `/etc/orbbec-streamer/live.yaml`               | The server's config. On upgrade, `apt` asks whether to keep your edited version; see [Upgrade](#upgrade). See [Configuration](/docs/server/configuration).                                                                                                                                    |
| `/etc/orbbec-streamer/tls/`, `tls.conf`        | Certificates and their settings                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| `/var/lib/orbbec-streamer/`                    | Engine cache and calibration; from poc.6 also `crash/`, where the WebTransport gateway writes a crash file if it crashes; `orbbec-streamer-report` collects the newest three. It needs `serving.crash_directory` in `live.yaml`, which a kept, edited `live.yaml` from an older version lacks |
| `/usr/lib/orbbec-streamer/bin/orbbec_streamer` | The server, also `orbbec-streamer` on the `PATH`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| `/usr/bin/orbbec-console`                      | The [terminal console](/docs/operator/terminal-console) (preview)                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| `/usr/share/orbbec-streamer/client/`           | The browser client and, in `operator/`, the Operator Console                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| `/usr/share/doc/orbbec-streamer/`              | Licences and notices                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |

| Service                  | Does                                                                                                                 |
| ------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `orbbec-streamer`        | Capture, GPU processing, encoding and the WebTransport gateway on `127.0.0.1:4443`                                   |
| `orbbec-streamer-web`    | Serves the client on `http://127.0.0.1:8080`, on this PC only                                                        |
| `orbbec-tls-renew.timer` | Renews the certificates. From poc.6 the server reloads them without a restart; from v0.1.5 the page server does too. |

Check them with `systemctl status orbbec-streamer orbbec-streamer-web`.

## Upgrade [#upgrade]

Install the newer package the same way:

```bash
sudo apt install ./orbbec-streamer_<version>_amd64.deb
```

Replace `<version>` with the new file's version, for example `0.1.5-1`.
Upgrading from a poc package works the same way. The packaged `live.yaml`
changed in v0.1.1 (a commented-out `network_probes` line), so if you edited
yours, the upgrade to v0.1.1 or later asks whether to keep it: keep your
version. It is unchanged from v0.1.2 to v0.1.5, so an upgrade from v0.1.1 or later doesn't ask.
From v0.1.3 camera poses are no longer mirrored in Y. A camera-pose
calibration committed on v0.1.2 stays valid and now shows correctly, but a
placement chosen while the scene looked mirrored may need placing again.
From v0.1.5 an upgrade keeps `orbbec-streamer-web` and
`orbbec-tls-renew.timer` disabled if you disabled them; up to v0.1.4 it
turned them on again. One exception when upgrading from v0.1.4 or earlier:
if every service the upgrade would turn on is disabled, the upgrade takes that for an earlier
`apt remove` and turns them on. From v0.1.5, `apt remove` followed by
`apt install` sets up like a first install: the server is enabled and
started with the cameras closed. Up to v0.1.4 it stayed off.
From v0.1.4 the default calibration board changes; see
[Calibration board](#calibration-board). The first upgrade from
poc.9 or earlier to v0.1.0-poc.10 or later enables and starts the server,
with the cameras closed. Later upgrades restart the server only if it was
running, and never change whether it starts at boot. Exception: if a
`live.yaml` you kept sets `serving.start_capture_on_launch: true` (cameras
open at every start), the upgrade keeps the previous state and prints
`left stopped: /etc/orbbec-streamer/live.yaml sets start_capture_on_launch:
true, so starting would open the cameras`.
Upgrading from poc.3 or earlier restarts it if it is enabled, which those
versions did on install. The certificates, the engine cache and your
calibration are kept.

<Callout type="warn">
  **`serving.console_origins` (from v0.1.0-poc.9).** The package's
  `live.yaml` lists the Operator Console's addresses under
  `serving.console_origins`. A server gives the
  [operator role](/docs/operator#the-operator-role) only to a page on one of
  them. If you keep an edited `live.yaml` from an older version, it has no
  such key. The server then starts as before, logs `serving.console_origins
    is empty: no session can be granted the operator role`, and every console
  session is a viewer: it can't change sensor settings or the stream
  profile or take over the setup lock. To get the role, add to the
  `serving:` section (each entry must also be in `allowed_origins`):

  ```yaml
  console_origins:
    - "http://127.0.0.1:8080"
    - "http://localhost:8080"
  ```

  **Downgrading** to a version before poc.9 with a kept `live.yaml`: delete
  the `console_origins` block first. The older server refuses to start with
  the unknown key. Downgrading from v0.1.0-poc.10 to poc.9 or earlier: also
  delete the `lan_viewers` line under `serving:` and restart; otherwise the
  older server refuses to start with `Unsupported serving key: lan_viewers`.
  Downgrading from v0.1.5 to v0.1.4 needs no change, but v0.1.4 turns disabled services back on and lacks
  the renewal fixes. Downgrading from v0.1.4 to v0.1.3, from v0.1.3 to v0.1.2, or from v0.1.2 to v0.1.1, needs no change, but
  without a `calibration.board` block, v0.1.3 and earlier expect the old 7 × 5 board. Downgrading from
  v0.1.1 or later to v0.1.0 or earlier with `network_probes` set:
  delete that line too (see [Active probes](/docs/guides/network#active-probes)).
</Callout>

From poc.4, placement commits are saved in
`/var/lib/orbbec-streamer/calibration/placement.json`. The upgrade moves a
poc.3 placement file there once, if you take the package's `live.yaml`. If
you keep an edited poc.3 `live.yaml`, the server keeps using
`/var/lib/orbbec-streamer/config/dev/placement.json`. To switch, add
`placement_path: /var/lib/orbbec-streamer/calibration/placement.json` under
`calibration:` and move the file while the service is stopped. If you edited `live.yaml` or
`tls.conf` and the new package changes that file too, `apt` asks which
version to keep.

<Callout type="warn">
  **Upgrading from poc.1 or poc.2 with an edited `live.yaml`:** keeping your
  version keeps the old `mask.rvm_engine_path`. The server then loads only
  that engine file and never builds one. If the file is missing, was built
  for another GPU or TensorRT, or the rig has two cameras, the server keeps
  running without background removal: the log has one error line with the
  cause and the fix, and the 5-second stats show `mask: failed`. Take the package's version and re-apply your edits, or fix the
  `mask:` section as in [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting).
</Callout>

### Calibration board [#calibration-board]

From v0.1.4 the default camera-pose board is a ChArUco board of 4 × 6
squares of 105 mm, with 79 mm markers, dictionary `DICT_4X4_50`. Up to
v0.1.3 it was 7 × 5 squares of 80 mm, with 60 mm markers, dictionary
`DICT_5X5_100`. The package's `live.yaml` names no board, so the server
uses the default. The **Camera pose** screen shows the board the server
expects; print that one.

To keep using a board printed for v0.1.3 or earlier, add it to the
`calibration:` section of `/etc/orbbec-streamer/live.yaml` and run
`sudo systemctl restart orbbec-streamer`:

```yaml
calibration:
  board:
    squares_x: 7
    squares_y: 5
    square_length_m: 0.08
    marker_length_m: 0.06
    dictionary: "DICT_5X5_100"
```

A camera-pose calibration you already committed stays valid either way;
the board matters only for the next run. See
[Camera pose calibration](/docs/server/camera-calibration#configuration)
for the keys.

## Remote viewers on the LAN [#remote-viewers-on-the-lan]

From v0.1.0-poc.10, browsers on other computers in the same LAN can view
the cameras. It is off by default: the page and the server listen on the
server PC only. The team has not yet tried it from a second machine. The
Operator Console stays on the server PC; a LAN viewer never gets the
[operator role](/docs/operator#the-operator-role).

The steps are in `/usr/share/orbbec-streamer/lan/LAN-VIEWERS.md` on the
server PC. In short:

1. Copy the page server's drop-in, so it also serves the page over HTTPS
   on port 8443. The page server then listens on all network addresses on
   port 8443, and its IP address allow-list is lifted:

   ```bash
   sudo mkdir -p /etc/systemd/system/orbbec-streamer-web.service.d
   sudo cp /usr/share/orbbec-streamer/lan/orbbec-streamer-web-lan.conf /etc/systemd/system/orbbec-streamer-web.service.d/lan.conf
   sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl restart orbbec-streamer-web
   ```

2. In `/etc/orbbec-streamer/live.yaml`, under `serving:`, set
   `listen_address: "0.0.0.0:4443"`, `lan_viewers: true` and
   `lan_page_port: 8443`, then run `sudo systemctl restart orbbec-streamer`.

3. If the firewall is on: `sudo ufw allow 8443/tcp` and
   `sudo ufw allow 4443/udp`.

4. On each viewer computer, trust the installation's certificate
   authority once. Download it on the server PC from
   `http://127.0.0.1:8080/.well-known/orbbec/ca.crt` (or copy
   `/etc/orbbec-streamer/tls/public/orbbec-ca.crt`). Check that
   `openssl x509 -in orbbec-ca.crt -noout -fingerprint -sha256` prints the
   same fingerprint on both computers, then import it as a trusted root in
   the viewer's system or browser.

5. On the viewer, open `https://<server-hostname>.local:8443` or
   `https://<server-LAN-IP>:8443`. The name or address must be one the
   server's certificate covers;
   `sudo /usr/lib/orbbec-streamer/tls/orbbec-tls status` lists them.

The page server's certificate is renewed with the others. From v0.1.5 the
page server picks up the renewed certificate by itself; up to v0.1.4, run
`sudo systemctl restart orbbec-streamer-web` after a renewal, or browsers
on other computers stop trusting the page once its old certificate expires.

To turn it off, remove the drop-in, set `lan_viewers: false` and
`listen_address` back to `127.0.0.1:4443`, and restart both services.

## Uninstall [#uninstall]

* `sudo apt remove orbbec-streamer` removes the programs and services and
  keeps your config, certificates and `/var/lib/orbbec-streamer`.
* `sudo apt purge orbbec-streamer` also removes the configuration and
  certificates the package created in `/etc/orbbec-streamer`, and
  `/var/lib/orbbec-streamer`, including the engine cache and calibration.
  Files you added to `/etc/orbbec-streamer` by hand stay, and so does the
  folder. From v0.1.5 purge also removes `*.dpkg-old` and `*.dpkg-dist`
  copies left by earlier upgrade questions. The certificates include the
  local certificate authority with its private key. A later install
  makes a new one, so every LAN viewer must trust it again; `remove` keeps
  it.

Both keep the `orbbec-streamer` user and group. The NVIDIA packages stay
installed; `sudo apt autoremove` offers to remove them.

## Collect a support report [#collect-a-support-report]

From poc.4, `orbbec-streamer-report` bundles the diagnostics into one
archive that you read and send yourself. It uploads nothing and changes
nothing:

```bash
sudo orbbec-streamer-report
```

**Expected result:** `orbbec-streamer-report-<UTC timestamp>.tar.gz` in the
current folder, readable by you. `--since "2 days ago"` widens the log
window (the default is the last 24 hours), `--out <file>` names the archive,
and `--print` lists what it would collect without collecting it.

The archive holds the package and system versions, the machine check, the
services' status and logs, `live.yaml`, `tls.conf`, the public certificate
data and, from poc.6, the newest gateway crash files. It never holds keys,
the contents of `/etc/orbbec-streamer/tls`, calibration or placement
files, or engines. Host names, IP and MAC addresses, e-mail addresses, your
user name and configured camera serial numbers are masked, but the masking
is pattern based: read the files before you send them. `MANIFEST.txt` lists
every file and what was masked.

## Troubleshooting [#troubleshooting]
